children.title: Graph Measurability
children.top_down_role: Measurability expressed through the graph of a multifunction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Section consequence intrinsic to graph measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\), then for every fixed \(y\in Y\), \[\{\omega:y\in F(\omega)\}=\{\omega:(\omega,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\}\in\mathcal A.\] Equivalently, \(\omega\mapsto\delta_{F(\omega)}(y)\) is measurable for each fixed \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable graph has measurable membership sections for every fixed range point.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\).
\(y\in Y\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{\omega:y\in F(\omega)\}\in\mathcal A\).

notation.meaning: Extended-real indicator of the value set

knowledge_statements.title: Measurability of Fixed-Value Membership Sections

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\((Y,\mathcal B(Y))\) is a measurable space with its Borel sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-sigma-algebra definition for a multifunction into a Borel space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multifunction \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\), define its graph by \[\operatorname{gph}F:=\{(\omega,y)\in\Omega\times Y:y\in F(\omega)\}.\] The multifunction is graph measurable when \(\operatorname{gph}F\) belongs to the product sigma-algebra \(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\). This property concerns joint measurability of membership pairs and does not, without additional hypotheses, assert measurability of projections of the graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is graph measurable when the set of parameter-value pairs belonging to its values is measurable in the product sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph Measurability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Graph Measurability leaf, and the statement is mathematically precise, but no inspectable citation or authoritative locator is supplied.

children.title: Inverse-Image Measurability
children.top_down_role: Measurability expressed through inverse images of range-space sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-valued separable-metric characterization of Effros measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be separable metric and let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed values. Then \(F\) is Effros measurable if and only if, for every \(y\in Y\), the function \[\omega\mapsto d(y,F(\omega))\] is \(\mathcal A\)-measurable. It is enough to test \(y\) in a fixed countable dense subset of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed values in a separable metric space, hit measurability is equivalent to measurability of point-to-value-set distance functions.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a separable metric space.
\(F\) has nonempty closed values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is Effros measurable}\iff d(y,F(\cdot))\text{ is measurable for every }y\in Y\).

notation.meaning: Distance from a point to the multifunction value

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Characterization of Hit Measurability

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(Y\) is a topological space equipped with \(\mathcal B(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-}(O)\in\mathcal A\) for every open set \(O\subset Y\).

notation.meaning: Hit inverse image of a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effros, or hit, measurability; this is not ordinary inverse-image notation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a multifunction \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) and a set \(B\subset Y\), its hit inverse image is \[F^{-}(B):=\{\omega\in\Omega:F(\omega)\cap B\neq\varnothing\}.\] The multifunction is inverse-image measurable, also called Effros measurable, when \(F^{-}(O)\in\mathcal A\) for every open set \(O\subset Y\). If \(Y\) is second countable, it suffices to verify this condition on a countable base of its topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction is inverse-image measurable when the parameters whose values meet any open set form a measurable set.
knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Measurability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hit-inverse-image definition, countable-base observation, and definition content kind fit the leaf, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Representation Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Range-space and value-set settings where the two representations coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Borel Graphs Give Universally Measurable Hit Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-to-hit implication after universal completion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) and \(Y\) be standard Borel spaces and let \(B=\operatorname{gph}F\subset S\times Y\) be Borel. For every Borel set \(C\subset Y\), \[F^{-}(C)=\operatorname{proj}_S\bigl(B\cap(S\times C)\bigr)\] is analytic and therefore universally measurable. Consequently, relative to the universal completion of \(\mathcal B(S)\), every Borel-graph multifunction is hit measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Borel graph has analytic hit projections, so graph measurability implies hit measurability after universal completion of the domain.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and \(Y\) are standard Borel spaces.
\(\operatorname{gph}F\) is Borel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^{-}(C)\) is universally measurable for every Borel \(C\subset Y\).

notation.meaning: Hit inverse image of the set

knowledge_statements.title: Borel Graphs Give Universally Measurable Hit Sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Valued Hit Measurability Implies Graph Measurability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hit-to-graph implication for a Polish range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) be a measurable space, let \(Y\) be Polish, and let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed values. If \(F\) is Effros measurable, then \[\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed-valued Effros-measurable multifunction into a Polish space has a measurable graph.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is Polish.
\(F\) is nonempty closed-valued and Effros measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Valued Hit Measurability Implies Graph Measurability

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a standard Borel space and \(\mathcal A\) is the completion of its Borel sigma-algebra under a probability measure.
\(Y\) is Polish.
\(F:S\rightrightarrows Y\) has nonempty closed values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is Effros measurable if and only if \(\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completed standard-Borel regime with a Polish range and closed fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be standard Borel, let \(\mathcal A\) be the completion of \(\mathcal B(S)\) under a probability measure, and let \(Y\) be Polish. For every nonempty closed-valued multifunction \(F:S\rightrightarrows Y\), the following are equivalent: \(F^{-}(O)\in\mathcal A\) for every open \(O\subset Y\), and \(\operatorname{gph}F\in\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(Y)\). The closed-fiber and completed standard-Borel hypotheses ensure that the relevant graph sections and projections remain measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For closed-valued multifunctions on a completed standard Borel probability space with Polish range, graph and hit measurability coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Equivalence Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A theorem is the appropriate content kind for this equivalence-regime leaf. However, the exact equivalence involving a completed domain sigma-algebra and the product sigma-algebra depends delicately on the stated measurable-space hypotheses and requires an authoritative theorem locator before the version can be accepted.

children.title: Representation Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where graph-based and inverse-image criteria require distinct treatment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hit Measurability Does Not Control Nonclosed Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hit-to-graph separation caused by dense nonclosed values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega=\{0,1\}\) carry the trivial sigma-algebra \(\{\varnothing,\Omega\}\), let \(Y=\mathbb R\), and choose \(a\in\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q\). Define \(F(0)=\mathbb Q\) and \(F(1)=\mathbb Q\cup\{a\}\). Every nonempty open set meets both values, so \(F^{-}(O)=\Omega\) for every nonempty open \(O\), and \(F\) is Effros measurable. However, \(\{\omega:a\in F(\omega)\}=\{1\}\notin\mathcal A\); hence \(\operatorname{gph}F\notin\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense nonclosed values can make all open hit sets trivial while hiding a nonmeasurable membership section, so hit measurability need not imply graph measurability.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) carries the trivial sigma-algebra.
\(a\notin\mathbb Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is Effros measurable but not graph measurable.

notation.meaning: Fixed irrational point distinguishing the two values

knowledge_statements.title: Hit Measurability Does Not Control Nonclosed Graphs

assumptions_latex: \(S=Y=\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}\) carry their standard Borel sigma-algebras.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Graph measurability need not imply inverse-image measurability when fiber regularity or completion assumptions are absent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection obstruction on an uncompleted standard Borel space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a Borel set \(B\subset S\times Y\), with \(S=Y=\mathbb N^{\mathbb N}\), whose projection \(\operatorname{proj}_S B\) is analytic but not Borel. Define \(F(s):=B_s=\{y:(s,y)\in B\}\). Then \(\operatorname{gph}F=B\) is Borel measurable, whereas \[F^{-}(Y)=\{s:F(s)\neq\varnothing\}=\operatorname{proj}_S B\] is not Borel. Thus graph measurability alone does not imply inverse-image measurability; closed fibers, suitable projection hypotheses, or completion of the domain sigma-algebra are substantive requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Borel graph can have a non-Borel projection, so graph measurability alone need not yield hit measurability.
knowledge_statements.title: Representation Separation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The projection counterexample correctly expresses a representation-separation boundary, and failure_boundary is the correct content kind. The existence of the specified Borel set with analytic non-Borel projection is the essential nontrivial claim and has no cited source.

children.title: Closed-Valued Measurable Mappings
children.top_down_role: Measurable multifunctions whose values are closed sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonemptiness and range-regularity boundaries of the standard selection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Closed-valuedness permits empty fibers, which preclude a selection. Open-hit measurability and nonempty closed values in an arbitrary topological range do not by themselves fall under the Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski theorem; Polish or an appropriate standard-Borel range hypothesis is substantive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empty fibers prevent selection, and the standard measurable-selection theorem requires descriptive regularity of the range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(\omega)=\varnothing\Rightarrow\nexists f(\omega)\in F(\omega).
knowledge_statements.title: Selection Hypotheses Are Substantive

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable selection for nonempty closed-valued Effros-measurable mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y\) is Polish and \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) is Effros measurable with nonempty closed values, then there is an \(\mathcal A/\mathcal B(Y)\)-measurable map \(f:\Omega\to Y\) such that \(f(\omega)\in F(\omega)\) for every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed-valued Effros-measurable multifunction into a Polish space has a measurable selection.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is Polish.
\(F\) is Effros measurable.
\(F(\omega)\) is nonempty and closed for every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f:\Omega\to Y\text{ measurable with }f(\omega)\in F(\omega)\ \forall\omega.
knowledge_statements.title: Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski Selection Theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent tests for nonempty closed-valued multifunctions in a Polish range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be Polish and let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed values. Effros measurability of \(F\) is equivalent to measurability of \(\omega\mapsto d(y,F(\omega))\) for every \(y\in Y\), and also to the existence of measurable selections \((f_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying \(F(\omega)=\overline{\{f_n(\omega):n\ge1\}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed values in a Polish space, open-hit measurability, measurable distance functions, and a Castaing representation are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(Y\) is Polish.
\(F\) has nonempty closed values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is Effros measurable}\iff d(y,F(\cdot))\text{ is measurable for every }y\iff F\text{ admits a Castaing representation}.

notation.meaning: Distance from y to the fiber

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Valued Measurability Equivalences

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(Y\) is a topological space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\omega)\) is closed for every \(\omega\), and \(F^{-}(O)\in\mathcal A\) for every open \(O\subset Y\).

notation.meaning: Hit inverse image of an open set

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multifunction \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) is closed-valued measurable when each value \(F(\omega)\) is closed in \(Y\) and, for every open set \(O\subset Y\), \[F^{-}(O)=\{\omega\in\Omega:F(\omega)\cap O\neq\varnothing\}\in\mathcal A.\] Nonemptiness is an additional convention and is not implied by closed-valuedness, since the empty set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed-valued measurable multifunction has closed fibers and measurable hit inverse images of all open subsets of its range.

children.title: Compact-Valued Measurable Mappings
children.top_down_role: Measurable multifunctions whose values are compact sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Noncompact Fibers Need Not Give Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of continuous maximum attainment without compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=[0,\infty)\) and \(g(x)=1-e^{-x}\), the set \(C\) is closed and \(g\) is continuous, but \(\sup_{x\in C}g(x)=1\) is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous objective need not attain its supremum on a closed noncompact fiber.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in[0,\infty)}(1-e^{-x})=1\text{ and }1-e^{-x}<1\ \forall x.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Noncompact Fibers Need Not Give Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise distance attainment and measurable nearest-point selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F(\omega)\) is nonempty compact in a metric space, then \(d(y,F(\omega))=\min_{z\in F(\omega)}d(y,z)\), and the nearest-point set is nonempty compact. If the range is Polish and \(F\) is measurable, this nearest-point multifunction is measurable and admits a measurable selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a nonempty compact fiber is attained, and under Polish measurable data a nearest point can be selected measurably.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has nonempty compact values in a metric space.
For the measurable conclusion, the range is Polish and \(F\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in F(\omega)}d(y,z)\ne\varnothing,\text{ with a measurable selection under the additional hypotheses}.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Fiber Distance Attainment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measurable Maximum Theorem for Compact Fibers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measurable values and optimizers for Carathéodory objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be Polish, let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) be nonempty compact-valued and Effros measurable, and let \(g:\Omega\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be Carathéodory. Then \(v(\omega)=\max_{y\in F(\omega)}g(\omega,y)\) is measurable, the argmax mapping is nonempty compact-valued and measurable, and it admits a measurable selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Carathéodory objective over nonempty compact measurable fibers has a measurable maximum value and a measurable maximizer.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is Polish.
\(F\) is nonempty compact-valued and Effros measurable.
\(g\) is real-valued Carathéodory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\text{ is measurable and }\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in F(\omega)}g(\omega,y)\text{ admits a measurable selection}.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Maximum Theorem for Compact Fibers

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(Y\) is a topological space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\omega)\) is compact for every \(\omega\), and \(F^{-}(O)\in\mathcal A\) for every open \(O\subset Y\).

children.title: Value-Set Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: Changes in measurability and selection behavior across value-set compactness regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundedness Does Not Replace Total Boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional obstruction to the finite-dimensional compactness upgrade.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In every infinite-dimensional normed space \(X\), the closed unit ball \(\overline B_X\) is closed and bounded but not norm compact. Hence boundedness cannot replace total boundedness in the closed-to-compact transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed bounded fibers need not be norm compact in infinite-dimensional spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an infinite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \overline B_X\text{ is closed and bounded but not norm compact}.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundedness Does Not Replace Total Boundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact metric threshold upgrading closed fibers to compact fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a complete metric space, a set is compact if and only if it is closed and totally bounded. Consequently, if every fiber of \(F\) is closed, then \(F\) is compact-valued exactly when every fiber is totally bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a complete metric range, total boundedness is exactly the additional fiber condition needed to upgrade closed values to compact values.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is a complete metric space.
Every \(F(\omega)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(\omega)\text{ is compact}\iff F(\omega)\text{ is totally bounded}\quad\forall\omega.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete-Metric Compactness Transition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise weak compactness alternative in reflexive Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is reflexive, every norm-closed bounded convex subset of \(X\) is weakly compact. Thus norm-closed bounded convex fibers are compact in the weak topology, although they need not be norm compact. This fiberwise conclusion alone makes no assertion that norm-Effros measurability is equivalent to weak-Effros measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reflexivity upgrades closed bounded convex fibers to weak compactness, but neither to norm compactness nor automatically to weak measurability.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a reflexive Banach space.
Each fiber is norm closed, bounded, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(\omega)\text{ is weakly compact for every }\omega.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Topology Compactness Upgrade

assumptions_latex: \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) is inverse-image measurable.
\(Y\) is Hausdorff.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compact-valuedness implies closed-valuedness; the converse generally fails, but holds for closed bounded fibers in finite-dimensional normed spaces.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of a normed space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transition between compact and closed fiber regimes.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Y\) is Hausdorff, every compact-valued measurable multifunction is closed-valued measurable. For \(Y=\mathbb R^d\), a closed-valued multifunction whose fibers are bounded is compact-valued by finite-dimensional compactness. This transition fails in an infinite-dimensional normed space \(X\): the constant multifunction \(F(\omega)=\overline B_X\) is measurable and has closed bounded values, while \(\overline B_X\) is not compact when \(X\) is infinite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact fibers are closed in Hausdorff spaces; closed bounded fibers become compact in finite dimensions, but not in infinite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Value-Set Regime Transitions

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Set-Valued Mappings p. 148
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis

children.title: Measurable Selection Principles
children.top_down_role: Selection theorem families connecting measurable sets with measurable decisions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable-selector representation of closed-valued measurable multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\) be Polish and let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed values. Then \(F\) is Effros measurable if and only if there exist measurable selections \(f_n:\Omega\to Y\) such that \[F(\omega)=\overline{\{f_n(\omega):n\in\mathbb N\}}\qquad(\omega\in\Omega).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed-valued multifunction into a Polish space is Effros measurable exactly when it is pointwise generated densely by countably many measurable selections.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\) is Polish.
\(F\) has nonempty closed values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is Effros measurable}\iff F(\omega)=\overline{\{f_n(\omega):n\in\mathbb N\}}\) for measurable selections \(f_n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Castaing Representation Theorem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection principle for parameterized normal-integrand minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((T,\mathcal A,\mu)\) be complete and sigma-finite, let \(X\) be Polish, and let \(h:T\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a normal integrand. Put \(m(t)=\inf_x h(t,x)\). For every measurable \(\varepsilon:T\to(0,\infty)\), on the measurable set where \(m(t)\in\mathbb R\) there exists a measurable \(x_\varepsilon(t)\) satisfying \[h(t,x_\varepsilon(t))<m(t)+\varepsilon(t).\] If the argmin multifunction is nonempty, closed-valued, and Effros measurable, it admits a measurable exact minimizer selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal-integrand minimization admits measurable strict epsilon-minimizers, and measurable nonempty closed argmin sets admit exact measurable minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\mathcal A,\mu)\) is complete and sigma-finite.
\(X\) is Polish and \(h\) is a normal integrand.
\(\varepsilon:T\to(0,\infty)\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_\varepsilon\text{ measurable}:h(t,x_\varepsilon(t))<m(t)+\varepsilon(t)\) wherever \(m(t)\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Epsilon-Minimizer Selection

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(Y\) is Polish.
\(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) is Effros measurable with nonempty closed values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an \(\mathcal A/\mathcal B(Y)\)-measurable map \(f\) satisfying \(f(\omega)\in F(\omega)\) for every \(\omega\in\Omega\).

notation.meaning: A measurable selection of the multifunction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kuratowski–Ryll-Nardzewski closed-valued selection theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) be a measurable space, let \(Y\) be Polish, and let \(F:\Omega\rightrightarrows Y\) have nonempty closed values. If \(F^{-}(O)\in\mathcal A\) for every open set \(O\subset Y\), then there exists an \(\mathcal A/\mathcal B(Y)\)-measurable map \(f:\Omega\to Y\) such that \[f(\omega)\in F(\omega)\qquad\text{for every }\omega\in\Omega.\] Such a map is called a measurable selection of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty closed-valued Effros-measurable multifunction into a Polish space admits a measurable selection.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Selection Principles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is the Kuratowski-Ryll-Nardzewski measurable selection theorem with appropriate hypotheses, and theorem is the correct content kind for the topic. No authoritative theorem or page locator is supplied.

children.top_down_role: Normal-integrand structure represented through measurable epigraph mappings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint Measurability Does Not Imply Closed Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse without lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h(\omega,x)=\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}(x)\) on \(X=\mathbb R\) is jointly Borel measurable, but its state fiber is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\). Its epigraph is therefore not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint scalar measurability alone does not imply lower-semicontinuous fibers or closed epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{joint measurability}\centernot\Rightarrow\text{closed epigraphs}.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Measurability Does Not Imply Closed Epigraphs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar measurability implied by measurable closed epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is Polish and \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has lower-semicontinuous fibers and a measurable epigraph mapping, then \(h\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal integrand on a Polish state space is jointly measurable as an extended-real function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Polish.
The fibers are lower semicontinuous.
The epigraph mapping is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h:(\Omega\times X,\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X))\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Joint Measurability of Normal Integrands

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable measurable representation of nonempty closed epigraph fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under Polish and nonempty closed-epigraph hypotheses, epigraphical measurability is equivalent to measurable maps \((x_n,r_n):\Omega\to X\times\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\operatorname{epi}h_\omega=\overline{\{(x_n(\omega),r_n(\omega)):n\ge1\}}\) for every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measurable closed epigraph mapping admits a countable measurable dense family of epigraph points.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Polish.
Every epigraph is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}h\text{ is measurable}\iff\operatorname{epi}h\text{ admits a Castaing representation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Castaing Representation of Measurable Epigraphs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent scalar tests for a nonempty closed epigraph mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be Polish and suppose every \(h_\omega\) is lower semicontinuous with nonempty epigraph. Then \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is Effros measurable if and only if \(\omega\mapsto d((x,r),\operatorname{epi}h_\omega)\) is measurable for every \((x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R\). It suffices to test a countable dense subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed epigraph measurability is equivalent to measurable distances to epigraphs, with countably many tests sufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Polish.
Every \(h_\omega\) is lower semicontinuous.
Every epigraph is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}h\text{ is measurable}\iff d(z,\operatorname{epi}h_\omega)\text{ is measurable in }\omega\ \forall z.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance Tests for Epigraphical Measurability

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(X\) is a separable metric space.
\(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is epigraphically measurable when \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is a closed-valued measurable multifunction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph-multifunction formulation of normal-integrand measurability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), write \(h_\omega(x):=h(\omega,x)\) and \[\operatorname{epi}h_\omega:=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:h_\omega(x)\le r\}.\] The integrand is epigraphically measurable when the multifunction \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is Effros measurable. If every \(h_\omega\) is lower semicontinuous, these epigraphs are closed; the combination of closed epigraphs and epigraphical measurability is the normal-integrand condition in this setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand is epigraphically measurable when its parameterized epigraph mapping is measurable; lower semicontinuous fibers make those epigraphs closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Measurability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epigraph-multifunction formulation fits the leaf and is appropriately classified as a definition. The precise convention connecting Effros-measurable epigraphs, lower semicontinuous fibers, and normal integrands requires a cited definition or theorem locator.

children.title: Carathéodory Integrands
children.top_down_role: Integrands with measurable parameter dependence and continuous state dependence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the sectional-to-joint measurability implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The standard implication from measurable parameter sections and continuous state sections to product measurability uses separable metrizability, or a comparable countability hypothesis, for the state space. The sectional assumptions alone do not provide that conclusion for arbitrary topological state spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual Carathéodory joint-measurability theorem depends on a countability hypothesis on the state space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{sectional measurability and continuity do not imply joint measurability in arbitrary topological spaces}.
knowledge_statements.title: Separability Boundary for Joint Measurability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inclusion of finite-valued Carathéodory data in the normal-integrand class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a separable metric state space, a real-valued Carathéodory integrand is jointly measurable and has continuous, hence lower-semicontinuous, fibers. Its epigraph mapping is therefore closed-valued measurable, so it is a finite-valued normal integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued Carathéodory integrand on a separable metric state space is a normal integrand.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is separable metric.
\(h:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) is Carathéodory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\text{ is a finite-valued normal integrand}.
knowledge_statements.title: Carathéodory Integrands Are Normal

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable formulas for extrema of continuous state sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(D\subset X\) is countable and dense and \(h\) is Carathéodory, then \(\sup_{x\in X}h(\omega,x)=\sup_{x\in D}h(\omega,x)\) and \(\inf_{x\in X}h(\omega,x)=\inf_{x\in D}h(\omega,x)\). Consequently both extended-real extrema are measurable in \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiber extrema of a Carathéodory integrand can be computed on one countable dense state set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is separable metric.
\(D\subset X\) is countable and dense.
\(h\) is real-valued Carathéodory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_Xh(\omega,\cdot)=\sup_Dh(\omega,\cdot),\quad\inf_Xh(\omega,\cdot)=\inf_Dh(\omega,\cdot).
knowledge_statements.title: Countable Dense-State Extremum Formulas

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of a Carathéodory integrand along a measurable state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be separable metric, let \(h:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) be Carathéodory, and let \(x:\Omega\to X\) be measurable. Then \(\omega\mapsto h(\omega,x(\omega))\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluating a Carathéodory integrand along a measurable state gives a measurable scalar function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is separable metric.
\(h\) is real-valued Carathéodory.
\(x:\Omega\to X\) is measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \omega\mapsto h(\omega,x(\omega))\text{ is measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Composition Theorem

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(X\) is a separable metric space.
\(h:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(h(\cdot,x)\) is measurable and each \(h(\omega,\cdot)\) is continuous; consequently \(h\) is jointly measurable.

notation.meaning: Parameter section at a fixed state
State section at a fixed parameter

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued Carathéodory condition on a separable metric state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(h:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) is a Carathéodory integrand when \(\omega\mapsto h(\omega,x)\) is \(\mathcal A\)-measurable for every \(x\in X\), and \(x\mapsto h(\omega,x)\) is continuous for every \(\omega\in\Omega\). If \(X\) is separable metric, these two sectional conditions imply that \(h\) is measurable with respect to \(\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X)\). Its continuous fibers are lower semicontinuous, placing it within the finite-valued normal-integrand regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Carathéodory integrand is measurable in the parameter and continuous in the state; separability yields joint measurability.
knowledge_statements.title: Carathéodory Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sectional conditions correctly define a finite-valued Caratheodory integrand, while joint measurability is a consequence under separable metrizability. The definition content kind is acceptable for the leaf, but neither the definition nor the joint-measurability result has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Extended-Valued Integrands
children.top_down_role: Integrands representing pointwise restrictions and singular costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-definedness of indicator-augmented integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The sums \((+\infty)+(-\infty)\) and \((-\infty)+(+\infty)\) are undefined in standard extended-real arithmetic. Thus \(g+\delta_C\) is automatically well-defined when \(g\) is real-valued or never takes \(-\infty\); a general extended-valued \(g\) requires an explicit compatibility convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Indicator augmentation must avoid indeterminate sums of positive and negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g>-\infty\Rightarrow g+\delta_C\text{ is well-defined}.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Real Arithmetic Compatibility

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise admissible domain encoded by finite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an extended-valued integrand \(h\), define \(D(\omega)=\operatorname{dom}h_\omega=\{x\in X:h(\omega,x)<+\infty\}\). Thus finite values identify the effective domain, while \(+\infty\) excludes states from it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of each fiber is the state multifunction encoded by finite integrand values.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(\omega)=\{x:h(\omega,x)<+\infty\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Domain Multifunction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuity failure for an open feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\), the indicator \(\delta_C\) is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\) or \(1\). Hence measurability without fiberwise closedness does not make a constraint indicator normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of an open constraint set is not lower semicontinuous at its boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_{(0,1)}\text{ is not a normal integrand}.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Constraints Yield Nonnormal Indicators

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between measurable closed constraints and normal indicator integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be Polish and let \(C:\Omega\rightrightarrows X\) have nonempty values. Then \(\delta_C(\omega,x)=0\) for \(x\in C(\omega)\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise is a normal integrand if and only if \(C\) is closed-valued and Effros measurable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty constraint multifunction has a normal indicator exactly when it is closed-valued and measurable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Polish.
\(C(\omega)\ne\varnothing\) for every \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_C\text{ is normal}\iff C\text{ is closed-valued and Effros measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Normality of Constraint Indicators

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(X\) is a state space.
\(C:\Omega\rightrightarrows X\) is a constraint multifunction.
\(g:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) is real-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise constraints are represented by \(h=g+\delta_C\), where \(\delta_C\) takes the values \(0\) and \(+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Indicator integrand of the constraint multifunction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint representation by an extended-valued indicator integrand, with a real-valued base integrand so the sum is well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-valued integrand is a map \(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}:=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). For a multifunction \(C:\Omega\rightrightarrows X\), define \[\delta_C(\omega,x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C(\omega),\\+\infty,&x\notin C(\omega).\end{cases}\] If \(g:\Omega\times X\to\mathbb R\) is real-valued, then minimizing \(g(\omega,x)\) subject to \(x\in C(\omega)\) is represented pointwise by minimizing \(h(\omega,x):=g(\omega,x)+\delta_C(\omega,x)\). The value \(+\infty\) excludes infeasible states.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real indicator that is zero on feasible states and positive infinity elsewhere converts a pointwise constrained problem with a real-valued objective into an unconstrained extended-valued expression.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Valued Integrands

children.title: Convex Normal Integrands
children.top_down_role: Normal integrands with fiberwise convex structure and dual representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise primal-dual subgradient certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\omega,x,x^*\), \(h_\omega(x)+h_\omega^*(x^*)\ge\langle x^*,x\rangle\). Equality holds exactly when \(x^*\in\partial h_\omega(x)\), equivalently when \(x\in\partial h_\omega^*(x^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fenchel–Young equality exactly certifies a primal-dual subgradient pair in each fiber.
assumptions_latex: \(h_\omega\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_\omega(x)+h_\omega^*(x^*)=\langle x^*,x\rangle\iff x^*\in\partial h_\omega(x)\iff x\in\partial h_\omega^*(x^*).
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel–Young Equality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise Fenchel conjugation in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a convex normal integrand whose fibers are proper. Then its fiberwise conjugate \(h^*(\omega,x^*)=\sup_x\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-h(\omega,x)\}\) is also a convex normal integrand with proper fibers, and \(h^{**}=h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiberwise Fenchel conjugation preserves proper convex normal integrands, and biconjugation recovers the original fibers.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a finite-dimensional convex normal integrand.
Every fiber is proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h^*\text{ is a proper convex normal integrand and }h^{**}=h.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugacy Preserves Convex Normality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the usual conjugate and subgradient package without properness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h_\omega\equiv+\infty\), then \(h_\omega^*\equiv-\infty\). If \(h_\omega\) takes the value \(-\infty\), then \(h_\omega^*\equiv+\infty\). Thus the usual proper conjugacy and subgradient statements require proper fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Improper fibers make Fenchel conjugacy degenerate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h_\omega\text{ improper}\Rightarrow\text{the proper Fenchel duality package may degenerate}.
knowledge_statements.title: Improper-Fiber Degeneracy

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric representation of fiberwise convex subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional proper convex normal integrand, the multifunction \((\omega,x)\mapsto\partial h_\omega(x)\) has closed convex values and a measurable graph in \(\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fiberwise convex subdifferentials form a closed-convex-valued multifunction with measurable graph.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a proper convex normal integrand on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{(\omega,x,x^*):x^*\in\partial h_\omega(x)\}\text{ is measurable}.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Subdifferential Graph

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space.
\(X=\mathbb R^d\).
\(h:\Omega\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is a convex normal integrand when its fibers are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and its epigraph mapping is measurable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional proper convex normal-integrand convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integrand \(h:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is a convex normal integrand when each fiber \(h_\omega:=h(\omega,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and the multifunction \(\omega\mapsto\operatorname{epi}h_\omega\) is measurable. Its fiberwise Fenchel conjugate is defined by \[h_\omega^*(x^*):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}\{\langle x^*,x\rangle-h_\omega(x)\}.\] The normal-integrand framework supplies the measurable structure needed to treat these convex fibers and their conjugates parametrically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex normal integrand has measurable epigraphs and proper lower-semicontinuous convex fibers, with conjugates defined pointwise by Fenchel duality.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Normal Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind fits the leaf, and the record clearly states its finite-dimensional proper-fiber convention. Because conventions differ on whether properness is built into the term convex normal integrand, and because the measurable behavior of conjugates is only alluded to, an authoritative definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Measurable Integrand Construction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Constructions preserving measurability or normal-integrand structure.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Chapter 14.B–14.E: Preservation, Limit Operations, and Operations on Integrands

children.title: Lattice-Envelope Construction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Pointwise extremum and envelope constructions for integrands.

children.title: Lattice Extremum Operations
children.top_down_role: Pointwise supremum and infimum constructions for measurable integrands.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive convexity-preservation result for lattice suprema.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every \(f_i(t,\cdot)\) is convex, then \[x\mapsto\sup_{i\in I}f_i(t,x)\] is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary pointwise supremum of convex sections is convex.
assumptions_latex: Each section \(f_i(t,\cdot)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{i\in I}f_i(t,\cdot)\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Preservation Under Suprema

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Calculus for Pointwise Lattice Extrema
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph formulas for arbitrary suprema and finite minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any family \((f_i)_{i\in I}\), \[\operatorname{epi}\Bigl(\sup_{i\in I}f_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] For \(f_1,\ldots,f_k\), \[\operatorname{epi}\Bigl(\min_{1\leq i\leq k}f_i\Bigr)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\operatorname{epi}f_i.\] Consequently arbitrary suprema and finite minima of lower-semicontinuous sections are lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise suprema correspond to epigraph intersections, while finite minima correspond to finite epigraph unions.
assumptions_latex: The functions take values in \(\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{epi}(\sup_i f_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i,\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\min_{i\leq k}f_i)=\bigcup_{i\leq k}\operatorname{epi}f_i.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Calculus for Pointwise Lattice Extrema

assumptions_latex: \((T,\mathcal A)\) is a measurable space and \(X=\mathbb R^d\).
Each \(f_n:T\times X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is jointly measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_n f_n\) and \(\inf_n f_n\) are jointly measurable; if every section is lower semicontinuous, then \(\sup_n f_n(t,\cdot)\) and every finite minimum are lower semicontinuous.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Countable pointwise lattice operations on extended-real measurable integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a sequence \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), define the lattice extrema pointwise by \[f^{\vee}(t,x)=\sup_{n\geq1}f_n(t,x),\qquad f^{\wedge}(t,x)=\inf_{n\geq1}f_n(t,x).\] Both functions are \((\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal B(X))\)-measurable. If every \(f_n(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(f^{\vee}(t,\cdot)\) is lower semicontinuous. A finite pointwise minimum of lower-semicontinuous sections is also lower semicontinuous, whereas a countably infinite minimum need not be.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Countable pointwise suprema and infima preserve measurability. Suprema and finite minima preserve lower semicontinuity, but countably infinite minima may not.
knowledge_statements.title: Lattice Extremum Operations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the leaf and is mathematically standard, but no inspectable citation supports the preservation and failure claims.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convexity preservation under pointwise minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pointwise supremum of any family of convex functions is convex. A pointwise minimum of convex functions need not be convex; for example, \[\min\{(x-1)^2,(x+1)^2\}\] is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Suprema preserve convexity, whereas even finite minima generally do not.
assumptions_latex: Each function in the supremum family is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_i f_i\text{ is convex, while finite infima need not be convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Boundary for Lattice Extrema

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory covers pointwise extrema, countable measurability, lower-semicontinuity thresholds, epigraph formulas, and convexity preservation under suprema. Essential envelopes were excluded as sibling content; concrete measurability, lower-semicontinuity, and convexity failures were assigned to Operation Preservation Boundaries.

children.title: Measurable Envelope Constructions
children.top_down_role: Envelope constructions retaining measurable-integrand structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic lower envelopes modulo almost-everywhere equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every family \(\{f_i:i\in I\}\subset L^0(S;\overline{\mathbb R})\), there is an essential infimum \(\ell\), unique almost everywhere, characterized by \(\ell\leq f_i\) almost everywhere for every \(i\) and maximality among measurable common lower bounds. Moreover, some countable \(I_0\subset I\) satisfies \[\ell=\inf_{i\in I_0}f_i\quad\text{almost everywhere}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every measurable family has an essential infimum represented almost everywhere by a countable subfamily.
assumptions_latex: \((S,\Sigma,\nu)\) is a complete finite measure space.
\(f_i\in L^0(S,\Sigma,\nu;\overline{\mathbb R})\) for every \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{ess\,inf}_{i\in I}f_i=\inf_{i\in I_0}f_i\quad\nu\text{-almost everywhere for some countable }I_0\subset I.
knowledge_statements.title: Essential Infimum and Countable Representation

assumptions_latex: \((S,\Sigma,\nu)\) is a complete finite measure space.
\(\{f_i:i\in I\}\subset L^0(S,\Sigma,\nu;\overline{\mathbb R})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a measurable essential supremum \(h\), unique almost everywhere, and some countable \(I_0\subset I\) satisfies \(h=\sup_{i\in I_0}f_i\) almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Space of measurable extended-real functions modulo almost-everywhere equality

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic upper envelopes, including reduction to a countable subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The measurable upper envelope of the family is its essential supremum \[h=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{i\in I}f_i,\] characterized by \(h\geq f_i\) almost everywhere for every \(i\in I\), and by \(h\leq g\) almost everywhere for every measurable common upper bound \(g\). Moreover, there exists a countable subset \(I_0\subset I\) such that \[h=\sup_{i\in I_0}f_i\quad\nu\text{-almost everywhere}.\] Thus an arbitrarily indexed measurable envelope has a countable measurable representative modulo null sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every family of measurable extended-real functions on a complete finite measure space has an essential supremum represented almost everywhere by a countable subfamily.
knowledge_statements.title: Measurable Envelope Constructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the envelope-construction leaf, but the countable-subfamily theorem for an arbitrary family requires an authoritative source with a precise locator.

children.title: Operation Preservation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of measurability or normality preservation under lattice and envelope constructions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Minima Need Not Preserve Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp convexity boundary for lattice minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \(f_1(x)=(x-1)^2\) and \(f_2(x)=(x+1)^2\) are convex, but \[h(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\] is not convex; indeed \(h(-1)=h(1)=0\) while \(h(0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even the minimum of two finite continuous convex functions can fail to be convex.
assumptions_latex: The functions are defined on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1,f_2\text{ are convex but }\min\{f_1,f_2\}\text{ is not convex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Minima Need Not Preserve Convexity

assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) with its usual topology.
Measurability is understood with respect to the stated Borel or Lebesgue sigma-fields.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncountable suprema can destroy measurability, and countable infima can destroy lower semicontinuity.

notation.meaning: Indicator taking zero on a set and positive infinity outside it

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failures beyond countable measurability and finite lower-semicontinuous minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subset\mathbb R\) be non-Lebesgue-measurable. Every singleton indicator \(\mathbf 1_{\{a\}}\) is measurable, but \[\sup_{a\in A}\mathbf 1_{\{a\}}=\mathbf 1_A\] is not measurable. Separately, each \(f_n=\delta_{\{1/n\}}\) is lower semicontinuous, while \[\inf_{n\geq1}f_n=\delta_{\{1/n:n\geq1\}}\] is not lower semicontinuous because its zero set is not closed. Hence arbitrary lattice operations require countability, closure, or measurable-envelope hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An uncountable supremum of measurable functions may be nonmeasurable, while a countable infimum of lower-semicontinuous functions may lose lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Operation Preservation Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexamples are coherent and the failure-boundary kind is correct, but neither example has an inspectable citation.

children.title: Transformational Integrand Calculus
children.top_down_role: Integrands produced by transformations, images, and elimination of variables.

children.title: Integrand Composition
children.top_down_role: Integrands formed through measurable or continuous transformations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fiberwise convexity and properness under affine inner composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(t,\cdot)\) is convex and \(\Phi(t,x)=A(t)x+b(t)\), then \(g(t,x)=f(t,\Phi(t,x))\) is convex in \(x\). If \(f(t,\cdot)\) is proper, then \(g(t,\cdot)\) is proper if and only if \(\operatorname{range}\Phi(t,\cdot)\cap\operatorname{dom}f(t,\cdot)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine inner composition preserves fiberwise convexity; properness additionally requires the affine range to meet the effective domain.
assumptions_latex: \(f(t,\cdot)\) is convex.
\(\Phi(t,\cdot)\) is affine.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp pointwise-limit failure for lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \[f_n(x)=\max\{0,1-n|x|\}.\] Then every \(f_n\) is continuous and \(f_n\downarrow\mathbf 1_{\{0\}}\) pointwise, but the limit is not lower-semicontinuous at \(0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the measurable pasting by \[(u\oplus_Av)(t)=\begin{cases}u(t),&t\in A,\\v(t),&t\notin A.\end{cases}\] Then \(u\oplus_Av\) is strongly measurable. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral functionals reduce to coordinate sums on countably atomic spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\Omega=\bigsqcup_{k\geq1}A_k\) modulo null sets, where each \(A_k\) is a finite-measure atom, and let \(u=x_k\) almost everywhere on \(A_k\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-space specialization of an integral functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite-dimensional Euclidean space or a separable Banach space, and let \(\mathcal U\) be a specified class of measurable maps \(u:\Omega\to S\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-sensitive boundary of the rank-one-convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist finite continuous rank-one-convex integrands on \mathbb R^{3\times2} that are not quasiconvex. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional stationarity equation for a finite-order variational integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[J(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,j^ku)\,dx.\]
If f is differentiable in every jet variable, the coefficient fields f_{D^\alpha u}(x,j^ku) are locally integrable, and u is stationary under all \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^m), then
\[\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}(-1)^{|\alpha|}D^\alpha\!\left(f_{D^\alpha u}(x,j^ku)\right)=0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\Omega;\mathbb R^m).\]
With sufficient smoothness this holds pointwise and has order at most 2k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An order-k stationary integral satisfies the Euler–Poisson system obtained by applying the formal adjoint to each jet derivative.
assumptions_latex: f is differentiable in the jet variables through order k.
Each first-variation coefficient is locally integrable.
u is stationary under compactly supported smooth outer variations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{|\alpha|\le k}(-1)^{|\alpha|}D^\alpha(f_{D^\alpha u}(x,j^ku))=0\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: State-Dependent Jump Energies Require Two Traces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the single-representative polar formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A generic state-dependent singular formula cannot evaluate the jump part solely at a single value \(u^*\): on \(J_u\), the canonical data are the two traces \(u^+,u^-\) and the oriented normal \(
u_u\). Consequently a general state-dependent jump contribution requires a surface density depending on both traces, with orientation symmetry \(g(x,a,b,
u)=g(x,b,a,-
u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a jump there is no canonical single state value; general state-dependent jump energy must use both traces.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) has a nontrivial jump part.
The singular density depends on the state value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A generic jump term is not determined by }u^*\text{ and }dD^ju/d|D^ju|\text{ alone}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), \[Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+(u^+-u^-)\otimes\nu_u\,\mathcal H^{d-1}\!\llcorner J_u+D^cu.\] Thus \(D^su=D^ju+D^cu\), with jump and Cantor parts mutually singular; \(u\in SBV\) exactly when \(D^cu=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe energy decomposition for a prescribed gradient density and one-homogeneous singular density.

children.title: Recession-Energy Components
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic density structures associated with singular derivative energy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial recession convention when the asymptotic limit exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a density \(f(x,y,z)\), its strong recession function in the last variable is \[f^\infty(x,y,z):=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x,y,tz)}{t},\] whenever this limit exists. It is positively one-homogeneous in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong recession density is the asymptotic linear rate along a fixed gradient direction.
assumptions_latex: The displayed limit exists for every relevant \((x,y,z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty(x,y,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\infty(x,y,z)\quad(\lambda>0).

notation.meaning: Strong recession function in the last variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Recession Function

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust limsup convention when a strong radial limit may fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R\) with at most linear growth, define \[f^{\#}(z):=\limsup_{\substack{z'\to z\\t\to+\infty}}\frac{f(tz')}{t}.\] This function is positively one-homogeneous and upper semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper recession function records robust asymptotic linear growth under directional perturbations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) has at most linear growth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{\#}(\lambda z)=\lambda f^{\#}(z)\quad(\lambda>0).
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Recession Function

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Support Representation of Convex Recession
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conjugate-domain representation for a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function \(f\), its recession function is the support function of the effective domain of its Fenchel conjugate: \[f^\infty(z)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}(z)=\sup_{z^*\in\operatorname{dom}f^*}\langle z^*,z\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function's recession rate is the support function of the domain of its conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Support Representation of Convex Recession

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Recession Limits Can Fail under Linear Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between radial limits and robust upper recession envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(s)=|s|\bigl(2+\sin(\log(1+|s|))\bigr)\), the quotient \(f(t)/t\) oscillates as \(t\to\infty\). Hence \(f^\infty(1)\) does not exist, while \(f^{\#}(1)=3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear growth alone does not guarantee a strong recession limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{t\to\infty}f(t)/t\text{ does not exist},\qquad f^{\#}(1)=3.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Recession Limits Can Fail under Linear Growth

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Base-point-independent recession limit for proper closed convex densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex and \(z_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), then \[f^\infty(z)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(z_0+tz)-f(z_0)}{t}=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(z_0+tz)-f(z_0)}{t}.\] The value is independent of \(z_0\), and \(f^\infty\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex density, the recession rate exists, is base-point independent, convex, and one-homogeneous.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(z_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty(z)=\sup_{t>0}[f(z_0+tz)-f(z_0)]/t.

notation.meaning: Arbitrary base point in the effective domain.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) has at most linear growth in its last variable.
The displayed limit exists for every relevant \((x,y,z)\).

notation.meaning: Strong recession function of the gradient variable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong recession function, rather than the upper recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The strong recession function of \(f\) in its last variable is \[f^\infty(x,y,z):=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x,y,tz)}{t}.\] Whenever this limit exists, it is positively one-homogeneous in \(z\): for every \(\lambda>0\), \[f^\infty(x,y,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\infty(x,y,z).\] In linear-growth integral representations, this asymptotic density evaluates derivative components that are singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession density is the linear-rate limit of the integrand along large gradient directions; it is positively one-homogeneous and governs singular derivative energy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A first-order free-discontinuity functional has the form \[\mathcal F(u):=\int_\Omega f\bigl(x,u(x),\nabla u(x)\bigr)\,dx+\int_{J_u}g\bigl(x,u^+(x),u^-(x),\nu_u(x)\bigr)\,d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).\] The discontinuity set \(J_u\) is part of the unknown rather than fixed in advance; the first integral is bulk energy and the second assigns surface energy to jumps.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract prescribed-trace classes for a fixed ambient space and trace theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a function space with trace map \(T:X\to Y(\partial\Omega)\), and let \(R_\Gamma:Y(\partial\Omega)\to Y(\Gamma)\) denote restriction to a specified boundary portion \(\Gamma\). For prescribed data \(h\in Y(\Gamma)\), define \[\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}:=\{u\in X:R_\Gamma Tu=h\}.\] The choice \(\Gamma=\partial\Omega\) gives the full-trace class; a proper \(\Gamma\) gives a partial-trace class. Sobolev and \(BV\) variants arise by selecting their respective ambient spaces and trace maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trace-class variant fixes an ambient trace theory and prescribes the trace on all or part of the boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a function space equipped with a trace map \(T:X\to Y(\partial\Omega)\).
\(R_\Gamma\) is the restriction map to a specified boundary portion \(\Gamma\).
\(h\in Y(\Gamma)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}=\{u\in X:R_\Gamma Tu=h\}\), with full- and partial-boundary variants determined by \(\Gamma\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonemptiness criterion and affine structure of a prescribed-trace class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}\) is nonempty exactly when \(h\in\operatorname{ran}(R_\Gamma T)\). If \(u_h\in X\) satisfies \(R_\Gamma Tu_h=h\) and \(T\) and \(R_\Gamma\) are linear, then \[\mathcal A_{\Gamma,h}=u_h+\ker(R_\Gamma T).\] Thus arbitrary data in a larger boundary space cannot be presumed feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prescribed trace data are feasible exactly when they lie in the restricted trace range; a nonempty linear trace class is an affine translate of the zero-trace class.

knowledge_statements.title: Unilateral Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar one-sided obstacle constraints imposed almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a measurable lower obstacle \(\psi:\Omega\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), the lower unilateral admissible class is \[\mathcal K_{\psi}:=\left\{u\in X:u(x)\geq\psi(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\in\Omega\right\}.\] Similarly, a measurable upper obstacle \(\phi\) defines \(\mathcal K^{\phi}:=\{u\in X:u(x)\leq\phi(x)\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\in\Omega\}\). These are pointwise constraints with feasibility intervals \([\psi(x),+\infty)\) and \(( -\infty,\phi(x)]\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unilateral constraint requires a scalar-valued function to remain above a lower obstacle or below an upper obstacle almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an ordered space of measurable real-valued functions on the measure space \((\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)\).
\(\psi,\phi:\Omega\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) are measurable obstacle functions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit L2 projection for lower and upper scalar obstacles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\psi\in L^2(\Omega)\) and \(K_\psi=\{u\in L^2:u\ge\psi\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\), \(P_{K_\psi}v=v\vee\psi\). For \(\phi\in L^2(\Omega)\) and \(K^\phi=\{u:u\le\phi\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\), \(P_{K^\phi}v=v\wedge\phi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto a lower obstacle clips upward; projection onto an upper obstacle clips downward.
assumptions_latex: \(v,\psi,\phi\in L^2(\Omega)\).
The metric is the \(L^2\) norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal to a lower-obstacle set is nonpositive and supported on the contact set.
assumptions_latex: \(u,\psi,\xi\in L^2(\Omega)\) and \(u\ge\psi\) almost everywhere.
\(N_K(u)=\{\xi:\langle\xi,v-u\rangle\le0\ \forall v\in K\}\).

children.title: Constraint-Closure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Closure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure threshold for constant closed convex pointwise value sets in finite-measure \(L^p\) spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, then \[\mathcal K:=\left\{u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):u(x)\in K\text{ for }\mu\text{-almost every }x\right\}\] is convex, strongly closed, and weakly closed in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\). Closedness of \(K\) cannot in general be omitted: if \(K=(0,+\infty)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(0<\mu(\Omega)<\infty\), the feasible constant functions \(u_n(x)=1/n\) converge strongly in \(L^p(\Omega)\) to the infeasible zero function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex pointwise value set yields a strongly and weakly closed convex feasible class. Without closedness of the value set, even constant feasible functions can converge strongly to an infeasible limit.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)\) is a measure space with \(0<\mu(\Omega)<\infty\).
\(1\leq p<\infty\).
\(K\subset\mathbb R^m\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal K=\{u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):u(x)\in K\ \mu\text{-a.e.}\}\) is convex, strongly closed, and weakly closed; nonclosed \(K\) need not yield a strongly closed feasible class.

knowledge_statements.title: Differential Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sobolev fields subject to an almost-everywhere differential inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d,m,q\in\mathbb N\), \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), \(1\le p\le\infty\), and let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) be open. Given a differential operator \(A:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\to L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^q)\) of order at most \(k\) and a multifunction \(K:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^q\) with measurable graph, the differentially constrained admissible class is
\[
\mathcal A_{A,K}:=\bigl\{u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):(Au)(x)\in K(x)\text{ for almost every }x\in\Omega\bigr\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differential constraint admits the Sobolev fields whose image under the specified differential operator belongs almost everywhere to the prescribed measurable multifunction.
assumptions_latex: \(d,m,q\in\mathbb N\), \(k\in\mathbb N_0\), and \(1\le p\le\infty\).
\(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is open.
\(A:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\to L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^q)\) is a differential operator of order at most \(k\).
\(K:\Omega\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^q\) has measurable graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_{A,K}=\{u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m):(Au)(x)\in K(x)\text{ for a.e. }x\in\Omega\}\).

Then \(\ker A\) is a norm-closed linear subspace of \(X\) and is therefore weakly closed. More generally, \(A^{-1}(C)\) is norm closed when \(C\subset Y\) is norm closed and weakly closed when \(C\) is weakly closed.

children.title: Integral Constraints
children.top_down_role: Admissible classes restricted by subsidiary integral quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional moment constraints imposed on an infinite-dimensional decision field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m,r,s\in\mathbb N\). An integral constraint is a global feasibility requirement obtained by integrating functions of a decision field. For a class \(X\) of measurable maps \(u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\), its standard mixed form is
\[
\mathcal A:=\left\{u\in X:\int_\Omega g(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu\le 0,\quad\int_\Omega h(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu=0\right\},
\]
where the vector inequality is componentwise and the displayed integrals are finite. This aggregate condition does not require \(g(\omega,u(\omega))\le0\) almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral constraints impose integrated equalities or componentwise inequalities on aggregate moments of a measurable field, rather than requiring pointwise feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a finite measure space and \(m,r,s\in\mathbb N\).
\(X\) is a class of measurable maps from \(\Omega\) to \(\mathbb R^m\).
\(g:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^r\) and \(h:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^s\) are \(\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\)-measurable.
For every \(u\in X\), the components of \(g(\cdot,u(\cdot))\) and \(h(\cdot,u(\cdot))\) are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A=\{u\in X:\int_\Omega g(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu\le0,\ \int_\Omega h(\omega,u(\omega))\,d\mu=0\}\), with vector inequalities interpreted componentwise.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space of admissible fields.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_Q=T^{-1}(Q)=\{u\in X:T(u)\in Q\}\).

notation.meaning: Chosen homotopy, degree, winding, or homology invariant.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global feasibility specified by a chosen homotopy-invariant quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a particular topological invariant \(T\), such as a homotopy class, degree, winding number, or induced homology class, on the field space \(X\). A topological constraint with allowed values \(Q\subset Y\) defines
\[
\mathcal A_Q:=T^{-1}(Q)=\{u\in X:T(u)\in Q\}.
\]
The invariant and its domain are part of the constraint data: the expression is meaningful only where \(T(u)\) is defined, including any continuity, trace, or nonvanishing requirements needed by that invariant. Feasibility is global because fields agreeing locally may still have different values of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological constraint admits fields whose specified homotopy, degree, winding, or homology invariant lies in a prescribed set.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic inverse-image formulation fits the leaf, but no source establishes which invariant, domain restrictions, or topology are intended. Those choices materially determine whether the constraint is well defined.

children.title: Coupled Global Constraints
children.top_down_role: Problem classes combining integral restrictions with global geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Global Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global constraints jointly linking several fields or components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), let \(X_i\) be a decision-field space for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), and let \(Z\) be a target space. Given a joint constraint mapping \(G:\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\to Z\) and an admissible set \(C\subset Z\), the coupled feasible class is
\[
\mathcal A:=\left\{(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\prod_{i=1}^mX_i:G(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in C\right\}.
\]
The constraint is coupled when membership cannot in general be determined by testing each component independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coupled global constraint tests a tuple of fields through one joint mapping, so feasibility generally cannot be determined component by component.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb N\).
\(X_i\) is a decision-field space for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\).
\(Z\) is a target space and \(G:\prod_{i=1}^mX_i\to Z\) is a joint constraint mapping.
\(C\subset Z\) is the admissible target set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A=\{(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in\prod_{i=1}^mX_i:G(u_1,\ldots,u_m)\in C\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonclosed Equality Level of a Lower-Semicontinuous Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary sharp counterexample to equality-level closure under lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(G:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(G(0)=0\) and \(G(x)=1\) for \(x\ne0\). Then \(G\) is lower semicontinuous, but \(\{x:G(x)=1\}=\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous global constraint can have a nonclosed nonminimal equality level.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R\) carries its usual topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is lower semicontinuous but \(\{G=1\}\) is not closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure distinction between inequality and equality global constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(G:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(\{u:G(u)\le c\}\) is closed for every \(c\in\mathbb R\). Lower semicontinuity alone does not imply closedness of \(\{G=c\}\) or \(\{G\ge c\}\); continuity, or appropriate upper-semicontinuity in addition, is needed for those conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity closes global sublevel inequalities but does not by itself close equality levels or superlevels.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a topological space.
\(G:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous.
\(c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{G\le c\}\) is closed, while closedness of \(\{G=c\}\) and \(\{G\ge c\}\) does not follow from lower semicontinuity alone.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuity Closes Only Sublevels

assumptions_latex: \(X=L^2(0,2\pi)\) carries its weak topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality set \(\{u\in X:G(u)=\pi\}\) is not weakly sequentially closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-closure failure for a nonlinear integral equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(u_n(x)=\sin(nx)\) for \(x\in(0,2\pi)\). Then \(u_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^2(0,2\pi)\), while
\[
G(u_n)=\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin(nx)|^2\,dx=\pi
\]
for every \(n\), but \(G(0)=0\). Consequently,
\[
\{u\in L^2(0,2\pi):G(u)=\pi\}
\]
is not weakly sequentially closed. Thus weak lower semicontinuity of a nonlinear integral functional ensures closure of sublevel inequalities, but does not by itself ensure weak closure of its nonminimal equality levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oscillations can preserve a nonlinear integral equality along a weakly convergent sequence while the weak limit violates that equality.

children.title: Integration–Optimization Interchange
