children.title: Morrey Quasiconvexity
children.top_down_role: Vectorial gradient geometry governing weak lower semicontinuity.

children.title: Quasiconvex Integrands
children.top_down_role: The principal vectorial lower-semicontinuity class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cell representation of the largest quasiconvex minorant in the standard finite continuous coercive regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be finite and continuous with standard coercive \(p\)-growth. Its quasiconvex envelope is characterized by \[Qf(F)=\inf_{\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)}\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx.\] Under these hypotheses, \(Qf\) is the largest quasiconvex function not exceeding \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing cell energy over zero-boundary gradient perturbations produces the largest quasiconvex minorant.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is finite and continuous with standard coercive \(p\)-growth.
\(Q\) is a bounded Lipschitz reference cell.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed cell formula defines the largest quasiconvex minorant \(Qf\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Envelope by Cell Relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between quasiconvexity and weak lower semicontinuity for nonnegative autonomous gradient densities with p-growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be bounded and Lipschitz, \(1<p<\infty\), and let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty)\) be continuous with \[f(\xi)\le C(1+|\xi|^p).\] Then \[I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx\] is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) if and only if \(f\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous nonnegative autonomous density with p-growth, Morrey quasiconvexity is exactly the condition for sequential weak lower semicontinuity of its gradient integral.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is bounded and Lipschitz.
\(1<p<\infty\).
\(f\) is continuous, nonnegative, and has an upper \(p\)-growth bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous exactly when \(f\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Morrey Weak Lower-Semicontinuity Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is Borel measurable and locally integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconvex precisely when the displayed averaged-gradient inequality holds for every matrix and compactly supported smooth perturbation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morrey quasiconvexity for finite autonomous first-order integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The integrand \(f\) is quasiconvex if, for every \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and every \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), \[f(F)\le \frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f\bigl(F+\nabla\varphi(x)\bigr)\,dx.\] Equivalently, the affine map with gradient \(F\) cannot have its energy lowered by a zero-boundary oscillatory perturbation on a bounded Lipschitz reference domain. Under customary continuity and \(p\)-growth hypotheses, this condition is the central vectorial criterion for sequential weak lower semicontinuity of autonomous gradient integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex integrand assigns no lower average energy to any compactly supported gradient oscillation around a constant matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed inequality is the standard quasiconvexity condition, but local integrability of a merely Borel integrand does not transparently ensure every composed integral is defined. A source is required to settle the intended definition variant and the added equivalence and lower-semicontinuity claims.

children.title: Quasiconvexity Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Failure of weaker convexity notions to guarantee vectorial semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weakly convergent energy-lowering sequences arising from a failed quasiconvexity test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty)\) be continuous with \(p\)-growth. If for some \(F\) and \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), \[\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi)\,dx<|Q|f(F),\] then there exists a sequence \(u_j\rightharpoonup \ell_F\) in \(W^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), with the same boundary trace as \(\ell_F(x)=Fx\), such that \[\limsup_{j\to\infty}\int_Qf(\nabla u_j)\,dx<\int_Qf(F)\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Failure of one quasiconvexity cell test yields a weakly convergent sequence whose energy lies strictly below that of its affine limit.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous, nonnegative, and has \(p\)-growth.
The displayed zero-boundary quasiconvexity test fails at \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The associated gradient integral is not sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous at \(\ell_F\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonquasiconvexity Produces Weak-LSC Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Collapse in Scalar and One-Dimensional Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensional boundary for strict separation between rank-one convexity and quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m=1\) or \(n=1\), every matrix difference has rank at most one. Hence, for finite continuous integrands on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \[\text{rank-one convexity}\iff\text{convexity}\iff\text{quasiconvexity}.\] Strict rank-one-convex versus quasiconvex separation therefore requires \(m,n\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one convexity and quasiconvexity coincide for scalar-valued maps or one-dimensional domains; strict separation is genuinely vectorial and multidimensional.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is finite and continuous.
Either \(m=1\) or \(n=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one convexity, convexity, and quasiconvexity are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Collapse in Scalar and One-Dimensional Regimes

assumptions_latex: The matrix space is \(\mathbb R^{3\times2}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one convexity alone does not imply Morrey quasiconvexity and therefore cannot by itself guarantee weak lower semicontinuity of vectorial gradient integrals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Šverák-type separation in a genuinely vectorial matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite rank-one convex function \(f:\mathbb R^{3\times2}\to\mathbb R\) that is not quasiconvex. Thus, although \(t\mapsto f(F+t(a\otimes b))\) is convex for every \(F\in\mathbb R^{3\times2}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^3\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^2\), there are \(F\) and \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,1)^2;\mathbb R^3)\) for which \[f(F)>\int_{(0,1)^2}f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx.\] Hence testing only simple rank-one laminations misses more complicated gradient microstructures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In vectorial dimensions, rank-one convexity is strictly weaker than quasiconvexity and does not suffice for weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated 3-by-2 separation is a source-dependent Šverák-type result. Its exact finiteness, regularity, and implications for weak lower semicontinuity require a specific counterexample citation.

children.title: Polyconvexity
children.top_down_role: Minor-based sufficient structure for vectorial semicontinuity and existence.

children.title: Minor-Based Representations
children.top_down_role: Convex representations through gradient minors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic behavior of minor coordinates along rank-one lines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), every minor coordinate is affine along \(F+t(a\otimes b)\). Thus every selected minor \(D_k\) satisfies \[D_k(F+t(a\otimes b))=D_k(F)+t\beta_k\] for some constant \(\beta_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matrix minor varies affinely along a rank-one line.
assumptions_latex: \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each coordinate of \(M(F+t(a\otimes b))\) is affine in \(t\).
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Affinity of Minors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supporting-hyperplane form for a proper lower-semicontinuous convex representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(f=g\circ M\), where \(g:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then \[f(F)=\sup_{(p,c)\in\mathcal A}\bigl\{\langle p,M(F)\rangle+c\bigr\},\qquad \mathcal A=\{(p,c):\langle p,z\rangle+c\le g(z)\ \forall z\}.\] Conversely, every pointwise supremum of affine functions of the full minor vector is polyconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex minor representation is equivalently a supremum of minor-affine functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f=g\circ M\).
\(g\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) has the displayed supremal representation by affine combinations of minors.

notation.meaning: Affine minorants of the convex representative

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting Minor-Affine Representation
Minor-Based Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued polyconvexity through all gradient minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=\min\{m,n\}\), let \(M_k(F)\) denote the vector of all \(k\times k\) minors of \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and set \(M(F)=(M_1(F),\ldots,M_r(F))\in\mathbb R^N\), where \(N=\sum_{k=1}^r\binom{m}{k}\binom{n}{k}\). The integrand \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is polyconvex if there exists a convex function \(g:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[f(F)=g(M(F))\qquad\text{for every }F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}.\] Here \(M_1(F)=F\), and when \(m=n\), the highest-order minor is \(\det F\). Lower semicontinuity of \(g\) is an additional regularity condition, not part of this basic representation definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polyconvex density is a convex function of the full vector of matrix minors; lower semicontinuity of the representing convex function is an additional condition.
assumptions_latex: \(r=\min\{m,n\}\) and \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is polyconvex exactly when it admits a convex representation in the full vector of minors.

notation.meaning: Vector of all minors of orders one through \(r\)

children.title: Determinant-Sensitive Regimes
children.top_down_role: Polyconvex structures coupled to orientation and determinant behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Continuity Threshold for the Determinant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sobolev regime in which determinant minors pass to weak limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u_j\rightharpoonup u\) in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\) with \(p\ge n\). Then \[\det\nabla u_j\to\det\nabla u\] in distributions. If \(p>n\), the determinants are bounded in \(L^{p/n}\) and converge weakly in that space. At \(p=n\), the general conclusion is distributional; stronger \(L^1\)-type convergence requires additional equiintegrability. Below this regime, concentration can obstruct passage to the limit without extra control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At and above the natural Sobolev threshold, determinants pass to weak limits distributionally; stronger weak Lebesgue convergence holds above the endpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(u_j\rightharpoonup u\) in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\).
\(p\ge n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Determinants converge distributionally, and weakly in \(L^{p/n}\) when \(p>n\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Continuity Threshold for the Determinant

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower-semicontinuity boundary between nonnegative and strictly positive determinant constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: As functions of the determinant coordinate, \[\iota_{[0,\infty)}\ \text{is convex and lower semicontinuous},\qquad \iota_{(0,\infty)}\ \text{is convex but not lower semicontinuous at }0.\] In particular, for \(F_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,j^{-1})\to F=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,0)\), the strict-orientation indicator has value \(0\) at every \(F_j\) and \(+\infty\) at \(F\). A lower-semicontinuous strict-orientation model may instead use a convex barrier \(h\) with \[h(d)=+\infty\ (d\le0),\qquad h(d)\to+\infty\quad(d\downarrow0).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonnegative-determinant constraint is closed, while the bare positive-determinant indicator is not lower semicontinuous; strict orientation requires a barrier blowing up near zero.
assumptions_latex: The determinant is a coordinate of the full minor map.
Indicators equal zero on their constraint set and positive infinity outside.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closed orientation constraints are lower semicontinuous, whereas strict positivity requires a blow-up barrier to obtain a lower-semicontinuous density.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Versus Strict Orientation Constraint

assumptions_latex: \(m=n\), and \(M(F)\) includes \(\det F\).
\(g:\mathbb R^N\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The density \(f(F)=g(M(F))+\iota_{(0,\infty)}(\det F)\) is extended-valued polyconvex and enforces positive orientation.

notation.meaning: Indicator taking zero on the set and positive infinity outside

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued orientation constraint expressed in the determinant coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(F)=g(M(F))+\iota_{(0,\infty)}(\det F),\] where \(\iota_{(0,\infty)}(d)=0\) for \(d>0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Because the positivity constraint is convex in the scalar determinant coordinate, this formula is a polyconvex representation and gives finite energy only to orientation-preserving matrices. Weak lower semicontinuity of the associated integral additionally requires growth and integrability assumptions ensuring the relevant minors behave continuously under the chosen weak Sobolev convergence; these assumptions cannot be omitted merely from polyconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determinant constraints fit polyconvex representations, but weak lower semicontinuity also depends on growth and weak continuity of the minors.
knowledge_statements.title: Determinant-Sensitive Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-determinant indicator is convex as a function of the determinant coordinate and therefore gives a standard polyconvex constraint, but it is not lower semicontinuous at determinant zero. A source is needed to distinguish basic polyconvexity from the stronger lower-semicontinuity regime.

children.title: Rank-One Lamination Geometry
children.top_down_role: Rank-one directional geometry and laminated oscillation structures.

children.title: Rank-One Directional Geometry
children.top_down_role: Directional behavior along rank-one connected matrix states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-differentiable characterization of rank-one convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{m\times n})\). Then \(f\) is rank-one convex if and only if \[D^2f(F)[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]\ge0\] for every \(F\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable integrand is rank-one convex exactly when its Hessian is nonnegative in every rank-one direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^{m\times n})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is rank-one convex exactly when its Hessian is nonnegative on all \(a\otimes b\).

notation.meaning: Hessian quadratic form at \(F\) in direction \(H\)

knowledge_statements.title: Legendre–Hadamard Rank-One Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact compatibility criterion for two constant gradients across a planar interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a continuous piecewise-affine map have gradients \(F^+\) and \(F^-\) on the two sides of a planar interface with nonzero normal \(\nu\). Continuity across the interface holds exactly when \[F^+-F^-=a\otimes\nu\] for some \(a\in\mathbb R^m\). Conversely, every jump of this form admits a continuous two-phase affine construction across that interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two constant gradients meet continuously across a planar interface exactly when their jump is a tensor product with the interface normal.
assumptions_latex: The map is continuous and affine on each side of a planar interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^+-F^-=a\otimes\nu\) for some \(a\), and this condition is sufficient.

notation.meaning: Nonzero normal to the planar interface

knowledge_statements.title: Hadamard Jump Compatibility

assumptions_latex: \(F,G\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The segment joining \(F\) and \(G\) is a rank-one segment exactly when \(G-F=a\otimes b\) for nonzero vectors \(a,b\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of first-order compatible two-phase gradient mixtures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Matrices \(F\) and \(G\) are rank-one connected when \(\operatorname{rank}(G-F)=1\), equivalently \(G-F=a\otimes b\) for some nonzero \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\). A continuous function \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is rank-one convex when, for every such pair and every \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)F+tG)\le(1-t)f(F)+t f(G).\] Rank-one directions are precisely the jump-compatible directions for piecewise-affine gradients across planar interfaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one directions connect matrix phases whose difference is a tensor product and which can form compatible planar gradient mixtures.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Directional Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-one connection and rank-one convexity statements are standard, correctly formulated, and suitable for the directional-geometry container, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

children.title: Laminate Microstructures
children.top_down_role: Oscillatory structures generated through rank-one mixing.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Realization of finite splitting data by homogeneous piecewise-affine gradient oscillations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\delta_{F_i}\) be a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F\), and let \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a cube. There are piecewise-affine maps \(u_j:Q\to\mathbb R^m\) with \(u_j(x)=Fx\) on \(\partial Q\), \(u_j\to(x\mapsto Fx)\) uniformly, and uniformly bounded gradients such that \[(\nabla u_j)_\#\bigl(|Q|^{-1}\mathcal L^n\!\restriction_Q\bigr)\rightharpoonup^*\mu.\] Equivalently, \[\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q\psi(\nabla u_j(x))\,dx\to\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\psi(F_i)\] for every continuous \(\psi:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite laminate is generated by fine compatible piecewise-affine gradient oscillations having the prescribed phase fractions and affine boundary value.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F\).
\(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a cube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Affine-boundary piecewise-affine gradients generate \(\mu\) as a homogeneous gradient Young measure.

notation.meaning: Pushforward of the normalized volume measure by the gradient

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Laminate Gradient Realization

assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a compactly supported probability measure on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A laminate is a weak-star limit of measures generated by iterated barycenter-preserving rank-one splittings.

notation.meaning: Dirac probability mass at a matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous laminate measures generated by compatible sequential splittings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Begin with \(\delta_F\). Replace an atom \(\lambda\delta_A\) by \(\lambda[\theta\delta_B+(1-\theta)\delta_C]\), where \(0<\theta<1\), \(A=\theta B+(1-\theta)C\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(B-C)=1\). Each replacement preserves total mass and barycenter. Measures obtainable after finitely many replacements are finite-order laminates; compactly supported weak-star limits of such measures are laminates. Consequently every continuous rank-one convex \(h\) satisfies the Jensen inequality \[h(\bar\mu)\le\int h(F)\,d\mu(F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Laminate measures encode microstructures built through successive compatible rank-one phase splittings while preserving their average gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Laminate Microstructures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential-splitting representation fits the microstructure container, but defining all laminates as compactly supported weak-star limits and asserting the Jensen property require a source fixing the laminate convention.

children.title: Finite-Order Laminates
children.top_down_role: Hierarchical laminate constructions with finitely many mixing stages.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite combinatorial representation of a sequential laminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An atomic probability measure is a finite-order laminate exactly when it is the leaf measure of a finite rooted binary tree whose root is its barycenter and whose internal node \(A\) has children \(B,C\) satisfying \[A=\theta B+(1-\theta)C,\qquad 0<\theta<1,\qquad \operatorname{rank}(B-C)=1.\] Each leaf mass is the product of branch weights along its root-to-leaf path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-order laminates are exactly the leaf measures of finite barycenter-preserving rank-one splitting trees.
assumptions_latex: The probability measure has finite support.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite sequential splitting and finite admissible binary-tree representations are equivalent.

notation.meaning: Leaf mass determined by branch-weight products

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Splitting-Tree Representation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Jensen property inherited through finitely many rank-one splittings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i\delta_{F_i}\) be a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(\bar\mu=\sum_i\lambda_iF_i\). For every finite-valued rank-one-convex function \(h:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\), \[h(\bar\mu)\le\sum_{i=1}^N\lambda_i h(F_i)=\int h(F)\,d\mu(F).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite-order laminate satisfies Jensen's inequality for finite-valued rank-one-convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) is a finite-order laminate.
\(h:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is rank-one convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(\bar\mu)\le\int h\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Laminate Jensen Inequality
Finite-Order Laminates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive definition of atomic sequential laminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(F_0\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and set \(\mu_0=\delta_{F_0}\). A finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F_0\) is any atomic probability measure obtained after finitely many steps in which an atom \(\lambda\delta_A\) is replaced by \(\lambda\theta\delta_B+\lambda(1-\theta)\delta_C\), where \(0<\theta<1\), \[A=\theta B+(1-\theta)C\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{rank}(B-C)=1.\] Every such replacement preserves total mass and barycenter; consequently, every resulting measure \(\mu\) satisfies \(\int F\,d\mu(F)=F_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-order laminate is an atomic probability measure obtained through finitely many barycenter-preserving rank-one splittings.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every measure produced by finitely many admissible rank-one splittings is a finite-order laminate with barycenter \(F_0\).

children.title: Lamination Closure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Limits and closures of laminate-generated configurations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Escape-of-mass obstruction to barycenter preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^{1\times1}\), define \[\mu_j=\left(1-\frac1j\right)\delta_0+\frac1j\delta_j.\] Each \(\mu_j\) is a first-order laminate with barycenter \(1\), but \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\delta_0\), whose barycenter is \(0\). Thus narrow convergence alone does not preserve barycenters on unbounded matrix space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even first-order laminates can lose their barycenter when mass escapes to infinity.
assumptions_latex: Supports are allowed to escape every compact subset of matrix space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak-star convergence of probabilities alone need not preserve first moments or barycenters.

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at the scalar matrix \(t\)

knowledge_statements.title: Barycenter Loss Without Moment Control

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Passage of rank-one-convex Jensen inequalities through compactly supported weak-star closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subset\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be compact, let \(\mu_j\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)\) have common barycenter \(F\), and suppose \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\mu\). Then \(\mu\) is supported in \(K\), has barycenter \(F\), and satisfies \[h(F)\le\int_K h(A)\,d\mu(A)\] for every continuous rank-one-convex function \(h\) defined on an open convex set containing the splitting trees and \(K\). In particular, the assertion holds for every continuous rank-one-convex \(h:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactly supported weak-star limits preserve barycenters and finite-laminate Jensen inequalities when the test function is defined on the required rank-one segments.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is compact.
\(\mu_j\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)\) have common barycenter \(F\).
\(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limit preserves support, barycenter, and the stated rank-one-convex Jensen inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed Jensen Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noncompact replacement for the common-compact-support hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_j\) be probability measures with \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\mu\). If their first moments are uniformly integrable, \[\lim_{R\to\infty}\sup_j\int_{|A|>R}|A|\,d\mu_j(A)=0,\] then \[\int A\,d\mu_j(A)\to\int A\,d\mu(A).\] Consequently, a common barycenter is retained by the limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform integrability of first moments preserves barycenters under noncompact narrow convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu_j\rightharpoonup^*\mu\).
The first moments of \(\mu_j\) are uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int A\,d\mu_j(A)\to\int A\,d\mu(A)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Controlled Barycenter Stability

assumptions_latex: \(K\subset\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is compact.
All finite-order laminates under consideration are supported in \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lamination closure consists of weak-star limits of finite-order laminates and preserves probability mass, support in \(K\), and barycenter.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-support closure avoids loss of mass or moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the compactly supported lamination closure by \[\mathcal L(K)=\overline{\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)}^{\,*}.\] Thus \(\mu\in\mathcal L(K)\) when some sequence \(\mu_j\in\mathcal L_{\mathrm{fin}}(K)\) satisfies \(\int h\,d\mu_j\to\int h\,d\mu\) for every continuous \(h:K\to\mathbb R\). If all \(\mu_j\) have a common barycenter \(F\), then \(\mu\) also has barycenter \(F\). Every continuous rank-one convex function on a neighborhood of \(K\) obeys \(h(F)\le\int_Kh(A)\,d\mu(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compactly supported laminates arise as weak-star limits of finite-order laminates, retaining barycenters and rank-one-convex Jensen inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Lamination Closure Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compact-support closure statement is coherent and fits the container, but the exact closure convention and rank-one-convex Jensen assertion have no supporting locator.

children.title: Null Lagrangians
children.top_down_role: Variationally invariant densities and their role in minor structures and boundary dependence.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: General Variational Formulas and null-Lagrangian discussion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Piola Identity for the Determinant Minor
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservation law underlying boundary dependence of the determinant null Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cofactor of a gradient is divergence-free, making the determinant a divergence-form null Lagrangian whose integral is fixed by boundary data.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in C^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\); weaker distributional forms require suitable Sobolev integrability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The determinant minor is a divergence-form null Lagrangian and its integral is boundary-determined in the stated regularity regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Piola Identity for the Determinant Minor

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent variational characterizations of continuous autonomous first-order null Lagrangians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite continuous autonomous density \(L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(L\) is a first-order null Lagrangian; (ii) both \(L\) and \(-L\) are quasiconvex; and (iii) for every \(F\) and \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), \[L(F)=\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q L(F+\nabla\varphi)
\,dx.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous autonomous density is a null Lagrangian exactly when every zero-boundary quasiconvexity test holds with equality, equivalently when both signs are quasiconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) is finite, continuous, and autonomous.
\(Q\) is a bounded Lipschitz reference domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Null-Lagrangian, quasiaffine, and two-sided-quasiconvex formulations are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiaffine Characterization

assumptions_latex: \(L:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
\(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A first-order autonomous null Lagrangian is exactly an affine combination of minors, and its integral is invariant under fixed-trace variations.

notation.meaning: Minor using row set \(I\) and column set \(J\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of continuous autonomous first-order null Lagrangians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The density \(L\) is a null Lagrangian when, for every \(u\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(\varphi\in W_0^{1,\infty}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), \[\int_\Omega L(
abla u+
abla\varphi)\,dx=\int_\Omega L(
abla u)\,dx.\] Continuous autonomous first-order null Lagrangians have the representation \[L(F)=c_0+\sum_{k=1}^{\min\{m,n\}}\ \sum_{|I|=|J|=k}c_{I,J}M_{I,J}(F).\] Hence their integrals depend only on boundary trace data, subject to the regularity needed for the minors to be integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous first-order null Lagrangians are affine combinations of matrix minors, and their integrals remain unchanged under fixed-boundary variations.
knowledge_statements.title: Null Lagrangians

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The affine-minors classification is a nontrivial theorem and the representation content kind fits the container, but the classification and boundary-trace conclusion require a specific authoritative theorem or section locator.

children.title: Variational Convexity Separation Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Implications and strict separations among convexity, polyconvexity, quasiconvexity, and rank-one convexity.

children.title: Convexity Implication Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Implication structure among major convexity notions for gradient integrands.

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\in\mathbb N\) and \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{convex}\Longrightarrow\text{polyconvex}\Longrightarrow\text{quasiconvex}\Longrightarrow\text{rank-one convex}.\]

notation.meaning: Morrey quasiconvexity with compactly supported smooth variations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical hierarchy for autonomous finite-valued gradient integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Convexity means convexity on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). Polyconvexity means that \(f(F)=g(M(F))\) for some convex function \(g\), where \(M(F)\) is the vector of all minors of \(F\). Quasiconvexity means
\[f(F)\leq \frac{1}{|Q|}\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx\]
for every matrix \(F\), cube \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\), and \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\). Rank-one convexity is convexity of \(t\mapsto f(F+tA)\) whenever \(\operatorname{rank}A\leq1\). Under these conventions, the displayed implication chain holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity implies polyconvexity, which implies quasiconvexity, which in turn implies rank-one convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Implication Hierarchy

children.title: Strict Separation Phenomena
children.top_down_role: Regimes where neighboring convexity notions do not coincide.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-One Convexity Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-sensitive outer-link separation; the classical construction occurs on three-by-two matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite rank-one convex integrand \(f:\mathbb R^{3\times2}\to\mathbb R\) that is not quasiconvex. Consequently, \(\operatorname{quasiconvex}\Rightarrow\operatorname{rank\text{-}one\ convex}\) is strict in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On three-by-two matrix space, rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity.
assumptions_latex: The matrix space is \(\mathbb R^{3\times2}\).
\(f\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is rank-one convex but not quasiconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank-One Convexity Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-sensitive middle-link separation for quadratic integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite quadratic form \(Q:\mathbb R^{3\times3}\to\mathbb R\) that is quasiconvex but not polyconvex. Hence \(\operatorname{polyconvex}\Rightarrow\operatorname{quasiconvex}\) is strict in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quasiconvex quadratic form on three-by-three matrices need not be polyconvex.
assumptions_latex: The matrix space is \(\mathbb R^{3\times3}\).
\(Q\) is a finite quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is quasiconvex but not polyconvex}.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Need Not Imply Polyconvexity

assumptions_latex: \(m,n\geq2\), unless a more restrictive dimension is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{convex}\subsetneq\text{polyconvex}\subseteq\text{quasiconvex}\subseteq\text{rank-one convex}\), with strictness known for the indicated outer separations in suitable dimensions.

notation.meaning: The determinant of a square matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separations among convexity notions for matrix integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For square matrices of order at least two, \(f(F)=\det F\) is polyconvex, because it is affine in a maximal minor, but it is not convex; hence convexity is strictly stronger than polyconvexity. Moreover, in suitable matrix dimensions there exist finite rank-one convex integrands that are not quasiconvex, so the implication from quasiconvexity to rank-one convexity cannot generally be reversed. These examples show that the hierarchy does not collapse merely from continuity or finite dimensionality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Determinants separate convexity from polyconvexity, while specialized matrix integrands separate quasiconvexity from rank-one convexity in suitable dimensions.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Phenomena

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The determinant separation is standard, but the rank-one-convex/nonquasiconvex separation is dimension-sensitive and requires a specific authoritative source and exact matrix dimensions. The counterexample content kind fits the leaf.

children.title: Dimension-Dependent Collapses
children.top_down_role: Coincidences among convexity notions in special dimensional settings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic Collapse with One Matrix Dimension Two
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent coincidence for quadratic forms when the smaller matrix dimension is two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be a quadratic form and suppose \(\min\{m,n\}=2\). Then \[q\text{ is rank-one convex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ is Morrey quasiconvex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ is polyconvex}.\] In particular, for \(2\times2\) matrices a rank-one-convex quadratic form can be written as a convex quadratic form plus a scalar multiple of the determinant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic forms with one matrix dimension equal to two, rank-one convexity, quasiconvexity, and polyconvexity coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(q\) is a quadratic form on \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q\text{ rank-one convex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ quasiconvex}\Longleftrightarrow q\text{ polyconvex}.\)

notation.meaning: Value of the quadratic form on a rank-one matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Collapse with One Matrix Dimension Two

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ is convex}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is polyconvex}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is quasiconvex}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is rank-one convex}.\]

notation.meaning: Dimensions of the target and domain, respectively.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-valued or one-dimensional-domain gradient integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(m=1\) or \(n=1\), every matrix difference in \(\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank at most one. Consequently, rank-one convexity is ordinary convexity. Combining this fact with the general implication hierarchy yields equivalence of convexity, polyconvexity, Morrey quasiconvexity, and rank-one convexity for finite-valued autonomous integrands in these dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When either the domain or target is one-dimensional, the four standard convexity notions for gradient integrands coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Dependent Collapses

children.title: Regularity-Dependent Collapses
children.top_down_role: Coincidences induced by additional structural or regularity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse for finite quadratic forms on matrix space, independent of the matrix dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) be a quadratic form. Then \(Q\) is quasiconvex if and only if \(Q\) is rank-one convex; equivalently, \(Q(a\otimes b)\geq0\) for every \(a\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For quadratic matrix integrands, quasiconvexity and rank-one convexity coincide and are characterized by nonnegativity on rank-one matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(Q:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is a quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff Q\text{ is rank-one convex}\iff Q(a\otimes b)\geq0\ \forall a,b.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Quasiconvexity–Rank-One Convexity Collapse

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a bounded Lipschitz domain.
\(f:\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to\mathbb R\) is continuous and satisfies \(|f(F)|\leq C(1+|F|^p)\) for some \(1\leq p<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The quasiconvexity inequality tested on \(C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\) is equivalent to the same inequality tested on \(W_0^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collapse of smooth and Sobolev quasiconvexity tests under continuity and growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated continuity and \(p\)-growth assumptions, density of smooth zero-boundary maps in \(W_0^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\), together with continuity of the associated integral, gives
\[f(F)|Q|\leq\int_Q f(F+\nabla\varphi(x))\,dx\quad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(Q;\mathbb R^m)\]
if and only if the same inequality holds for every \(\varphi\in W_0^{1,p}(Q;\mathbb R^m)\). Thus these two test-regularity formulations of quasiconvexity coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity and suitable growth make smooth and Sobolev zero-boundary tests of quasiconvexity equivalent.
knowledge_statements.title: Regularity-Dependent Collapses

children.title: Integral Representation Theorems
children.top_down_role: Representation families for local lower-semicontinuous functionals.

children.title: Sobolev Integral Representation
children.top_down_role: Local functional representations on Sobolev spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued first-order representation under locality, measure structure, strong-Lp lower semicontinuity, and Sobolev growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1<p<\infty\) and \(F:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)\). Assume: (i) \(A\mapsto F(u,A)\) is the restriction of a finite Radon measure; (ii) \(F\) is local; (iii) for every open \(A\), \(F(\cdot,A)\) is sequentially lower semicontinuous for strong \(L^p\)-convergence on \(W^{1,p}\); and (iv) \[F(u,A)\le C\int_A(1+|u|^p+|\nabla u|^p)\,dx.\] Then there is a Borel integrand \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty)\) such that \[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx.\] The density has corresponding \(p\)-growth, and for almost every \(x\), \(\xi\mapsto f(x,s,\xi)\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local, measure-valued Sobolev functional that is lower semicontinuous in strong Lp and satisfies an integral upper bound has a first-order density quasiconvex in the gradient variable.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and open.
\(1<p<\infty\).
The stated measure, locality, strong-\(L^p\) lower-semicontinuity, and growth hypotheses hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx\) for a Borel density quasiconvex in its gradient variable almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Sobolev Integral Representation Theorem

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and open, and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(F:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to[0,\infty]\) is local, lower semicontinuous, measure-valued in its set argument, and has \(p\)-growth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a Borel integrand \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{m\times n}\to[0,\infty]\) such that \[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx.\]

notation.meaning: Open subsets of the ambient domain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order local integral representation on Sobolev spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume additionally that the growth bounds have the form
\[c|\nabla u|^p-C\leq F\text{ locally }\leq C\bigl(1+|u|^p+|\nabla u|^p\bigr)\]
in the standard integral-functional sense. Then a Borel density \(f\) exists for which
\[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx\]
for every \(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(A\in\mathcal A(\Omega)\). The density is determined up to equality for almost every \(x\) on values sampled by Sobolev jets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local, lower-semicontinuous, measure-valued Sobolev functional with suitable growth admits a first-order integral density.
knowledge_statements.title: Sobolev Integral Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A Sobolev integral-representation theorem is appropriate here, but phrases such as “measure-valued,” “has p-growth,” and “F locally” do not specify the required measure, locality, coercivity, and upper-bound hypotheses rigorously enough to validate the asserted representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Blow-Up Formula for the Sobolev Density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed small-ball density-identification formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The proposed record identifies \(f(x,s,\xi)\) through normalized localized minima with affine boundary data on shrinking balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed affine small-ball formula is a density-identification result rather than a representation theorem local to this leaf.
assumptions_latex: The Sobolev representation hypotheses and additional blow-up hypotheses would be required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Defer to the Blow-Up Density Identification Calculus sibling.}\)
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Blow-Up Formula for the Sobolev Density

intermediate_metadata.reason: The locally owned inventory is the first-order Sobolev integral-representation theorem with precise topology and growth assumptions. The Builder's affine blow-up record was deferred to Blow-Up Density Identification Calculus; BV representations and the general locality-measure mechanism were also excluded to sibling scopes.

children.title: BV Integral Representation
children.top_down_role: Bulk, jump, and singular representation regimes on BV spaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bulk, jump, and Cantor Radon–Nikodym decomposition without identifying the Cantor density as a recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), and let \(\mu_u\) be a positive Radon measure such that \[\mu_u\ll\lambda_u:=\mathcal L^n+\mathcal H^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}J_u+|D^cu|.\] The three measures in \(\lambda_u\) are mutually singular, so there are unique nonnegative densities \(f_u,g_u,h_u\), up to the corresponding null sets, such that for every Borel set \(A\subset\Omega\), \[\mu_u(A)=\int_A f_u\,dx+\int_{A\cap J_u}g_u\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}+\int_A h_u\,d|D^cu|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A BV energy measure dominated by the bulk, jump, and Cantor reference measures has a unique three-part Radon–Nikodym decomposition.
assumptions_latex: u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)
\mu_u\text{ is a positive Radon measure}
\mu_u\ll\mathcal L^n+\mathcal H^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}J_u+|D^cu|
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_u=f_u\mathcal L^n+g_u(\mathcal H^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}J_u)+h_u|D^cu|\text{ uniquely up to null sets}.

notation.meaning: Approximate jump set of the BV map.
Cantor part of the distributional derivative.
Localized energy measure associated with u.

knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Theoretic BV Energy Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measure Decomposition Does Not Identify the Cantor Density
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation between a three-measure decomposition and structural identification of its Cantor density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the local measure-valued functional
\[
F(u,A):=|D^cu|(A),\qquad u\in BV(\Omega).
\]
For every affine \(u\), \(D^cu=0\), so the density detected from affine bulk states is \(f\equiv0\), with \(f^\infty\equiv0\). Nevertheless, \(F(u,A)>0\) whenever \(|D^cu|(A)>0\). Thus locality and a Radon–Nikodym decomposition alone do not force the Cantor density to equal the recession function of the bulk density.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional charging only the Cantor derivative has zero affine bulk density but a nonzero Cantor density, so measure decomposition alone cannot identify the latter as a bulk recession function.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega)\).
No lower-semicontinuity or relaxation theorem is asserted for this example.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\equiv0,\qquad f^\infty\equiv0,\qquad F(u,A)=|D^cu|(A),

notation.meaning: Cantor part of the distributional derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Measure Decomposition Does Not Identify the Cantor Density

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical derivative decomposition furnishing the three reference measures used in BV integral representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\),
\[
Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^n+(u^+-u^-)\otimes\nu_u\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}J_u+D^cu.
\]
The absolutely continuous, jump, and Cantor measures in this decomposition are mutually singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every BV derivative splits uniquely into mutually singular absolutely continuous, jump, and Cantor parts.
assumptions_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^n+(u^+-u^-)\otimes\nu_u\,\mathcal H^{n-1}\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}J_u+D^cu.

notation.meaning: Approximate one-sided traces on the jump set.
Cantor part of the distributional derivative.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical BV Derivative Decomposition

assumptions_latex: \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), with \(Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^n+D^j u+D^c u\).
\(F\) is local, lower semicontinuous, measure-valued in the open-set argument, and has linear growth.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx+\int_{J_u\cap A}g(x,u^+,u^-,\nu_u)\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}+\int_A f^\infty\!\left(x,u,\frac{dD^c u}{d|D^c u|}\right)d|D^c u|.\]

notation.meaning: Approximate jump set of the BV map.
Cantor part of the distributional derivative.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bulk, jump, and Cantor decomposition of local BV functionals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the standard coercivity, locality, and continuity hypotheses ensuring BV integral representation, there are a bulk density \(f\), a surface density \(g\), and an appropriate recession density \(f^\infty\) such that, for every open \(A\subset\Omega\),
\[F(u,A)=\int_A f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx+\int_{J_u\cap A}g(x,u^+,u^-,\nu_u)\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}+\int_A f^\infty\!\left(x,u,\frac{dD^c u}{d|D^c u|}\right)d|D^c u|.\]
The three terms respectively charge the absolutely continuous, jump, and Cantor regimes of \(Du\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A suitable local BV functional decomposes into bulk, jump-surface, and Cantor contributions.
knowledge_statements.title: BV Integral Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: General BV representation theorems require detailed structural, continuity, coercivity, and growth assumptions. The identification of the Cantor density with the recession function of the bulk density is not justified by the stated generic hypotheses and needs a version-specific source.

children.title: Locality-Measure Representation Interface
children.top_down_role: Structural routes from local functionals to integral densities.

children.title: Functional Locality
children.top_down_role: Dependence of a functional on local agreement of admissible states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent factorization of a local functional through the almost-everywhere restriction class on each open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each open \(A\subset\Omega\), write \(u\sim_Av\) when \(u=v\) almost everywhere on \(A\). A functional \(F:X\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is local exactly when, for every open \(A\), there is a map \(\Phi_A:X/{\sim_A}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfying \[F(u,A)=\Phi_A([u]_{\sim_A})\qquad(u\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Functional locality is equivalent to factorization through the almost-everywhere restriction class on each localized open set.
assumptions_latex: F:X\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to(-\infty,+\infty]
u\sim_Av\iff u=v\text{ a.e. on }A
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is local}\iff \forall A\ \exists\Phi_A\text{ with }F(u,A)=\Phi_A([u]_{\sim_A}).

notation.meaning: Almost-everywhere agreement on the open set A.
Factor map on local restriction classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction-Class Factorization of Functional Locality

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to(-\infty,\infty]\), where elements of \(X\) are measurable maps on \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[u=v\ \text{a.e. on }A\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(u,A)=F(v,A).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locality with respect to almost-everywhere agreement on the localized set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The functional \(F\) is local if, for every \(A\in\mathcal A(\Omega)\) and every \(u,v\in X\), agreement \(u=v\) almost everywhere on \(A\) implies
\[F(u,A)=F(v,A).\]
Thus the value assigned to \(A\) depends only on the equivalence class of the restriction of the function to \(A\), not on values outside \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A localized functional is local when its value on a set depends only on the function inside that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Functional Locality

children.title: Measure Representation Properties
children.top_down_role: Measure-theoretic structure of localized functional values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute-continuity threshold for representing the localized measure by a Lebesgue density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(u,A)=\mu_u(A)\) for open \(A\subset\Omega\), where \(\mu_u\) is a finite Radon measure. Then \[\mu_u\ll\mathcal L^n\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists g_u\in L^1(\Omega):\ F(u,A)=\int_A g_u\,dx\quad\forall A\in\mathcal A(\Omega).\] The density \(g_u=d\mu_u/d\mathcal L^n\) is unique almost everywhere and, for almost every \(x\in\Omega\), \[g_u(x)=\lim_{r\downarrow0,\,B_r(x)\subset\Omega}\frac{F(u,B_r(x))}{|B_r(x)|}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure-valued localization has a Lebesgue density exactly when its representing measure is absolutely continuous, and that density is recovered almost everywhere by measure differentiation.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open.
\(\mu_u\) is a finite Radon measure representing \(A\mapsto F(u,A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_u\ll\mathcal L^n\) is equivalent to representation by the unique density \(d\mu_u/d\mathcal L^n\), recoverable by ball ratios almost everywhere.

notation.meaning: Radon–Nikodym density of the representing measure.

knowledge_statements.title: Radon–Nikodym Density Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\to[0,\infty]\).
For each fixed \(u\in X\), the set function \(A\mapsto F(u,A)\) is the restriction of a finite Radon measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For each \(u\), there is a unique finite Radon measure \(\mu_u\) satisfying \(F(u,A)=\mu_u(A)\) for every open \(A\subset\Omega\).

notation.meaning: Representing Radon measure associated with the function.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radon-measure structure of the localized set function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every fixed \(u\in X\), measure representation means that there is a finite Radon measure \(\mu_u\) on \(\Omega\) such that
\[F(u,A)=\mu_u(A)\qquad\text{for every open }A\subset\Omega.\]
Consequently the localized functional is monotone in \(A\), countably additive on disjoint Borel sets after extension, inner regular on open sets, and outer regular on Borel sets. The representing measure is unique because open sets determine a Radon measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each function, the localized energy extends uniquely to a Radon measure and inherits its additivity and regularity properties.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure Representation Properties

children.title: Localization Compatibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Agreement Gives Consistent Measure Restrictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility between functional locality and restriction of localized energy measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F\) is local and, for every \(u\in X\), \(F(u,\cdot)\) is the restriction to open sets of a Radon measure \(\mu_u\). If \(u=v\) almost everywhere on an open set \(A\subset\Omega\), then for every open \(B\subset A\), \[\mu_u(B)=F(u,B)=F(v,B)=\mu_v(B).\] Consequently \(\mu_u\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}A=\mu_v\mathbin{\vrule height 1.4ex depth -0.3ex width 0.07ex\vrule height 0.07ex depth -0.02ex width 0.8ex}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: States agreeing locally induce identical restrictions of their representing energy measures on that region.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is local}
F(u,U)=\mu_u(U)\text{ for every open }U\subset\Omega
u=v\text{ a.e. on the open set }A

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F(u,A)=\sup_{U\Subset A}F(u,U),\qquad F(u,A\cup B)=F(u,A)+F(u,B)\ \text{if }A\cap B=\varnothing.\]

notation.meaning: Compact containment of one open set in another.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of restriction, exhaustion, and disjoint localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F(u,\cdot)=\mu_u\) for a Radon measure \(\mu_u\), then restriction to an open subset is compatible with further localization: for open \(B\subset A\subset\Omega\), the restriction of \(F(u,\cdot)\) from \(A\) to \(B\) equals \(F(u,B)\). Moreover,
\[F(u,A)=\sup_{U\Subset A}F(u,U),\]
and for disjoint open sets \(A,B\subset\Omega\),
\[F(u,A\cup B)=F(u,A)+F(u,B).\]
These identities permit densities to be recovered from arbitrarily small neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measure-valued localization commutes with restriction, compact exhaustion, and addition over disjoint open sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Localization Compatibility

children.title: Nonlocality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Obstructions to local integral representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the measure property despite dependence only on values inside the localized set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scalar \(u\in L^1(\Omega)\), define \[H(u,A)=\left|\int_Au(x)\,dx\right|^2.\] For disjoint open \(A,B\subset\Omega\), \[H(u,A\cup B)=H(u,A)+H(u,B)+2\left(\int_Au\right)\left(\int_Bu\right),\] so whenever the cross term is nonzero, \(A\mapsto H(u,A)\) is not finitely additive. It therefore cannot be a representing measure or equal \(\int_A h(x,j^ku(x))\,dx\) for every open \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring an integral creates cross terms between disjoint regions, preventing measure representation even though the functional uses only values inside the localized set.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open.
\(u\in L^1(\Omega)\) is scalar-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The localization \(A\mapsto H(u,A)\) is generally nonadditive and has no measure or local-density representation.

notation.meaning: Squared integral of the field over the localized set.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonadditive Localization Obstruction
Nonlocality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise interactions across the boundary of a localized open set obstruct local jet-based representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) be bounded and open, let \(A\subset\Omega\) be open, and let \(K\in L^\infty(\Omega\times\Omega;[0,\infty))\) be positive on a subset of \(A\times(\Omega\setminus A)\) having positive product measure. For \(u\in L^\infty(\Omega)\), define \[G(u,A)=\int_A\int_\Omega K(x,y)|u(x)-u(y)|^2\,dy\,dx.\] Then there exist \(u,v\in L^\infty(\Omega)\) such that \(u=v\) almost everywhere on \(A\) but \(G(u,A)\ne G(v,A)\). Thus \(G\) is not local and cannot, for every open localization, be represented by a density depending only on a pointwise local jet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pairwise interaction that couples an open set to its complement can distinguish functions that agree inside the set, so it is nonlocal and has no purely local jet representation on every localization.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and open, and \(A\subset\Omega\) is open.
\(K\in L^\infty(\Omega\times\Omega;[0,\infty))\) is positive on a subset of \(A\times(\Omega\setminus A)\) of positive product measure.
\(G\) is defined on \(L^\infty(\Omega)\times\mathcal A(\Omega)\) by the displayed interaction integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists u,v\in L^\infty(\Omega):\ u=v\ \text{a.e. on }A\ \text{and}\ G(u,A)\ne G(v,A).\]

notation.meaning: The pairwise interaction energy localized in its first integration variable to A.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common rescaling architecture for volume and codimension-one measure components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the dilation \(T_{x_0,r}(y)=x_0+ry\), Lebesgue measure satisfies \(\mathcal L^d(T_{x_0,r}(A))=r^d\mathcal L^d(A)\), while \((d-1)\)-dimensional Hausdorff measure on a rectifiable interface scales by \(r^{d-1}\). Consequently, volume-density blow-ups use \(r^{-d}\) normalization and surface-density blow-ups use \(r^{-(d-1)}\) normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normalization in a blow-up is determined by the dimension of the reference measure whose density is being recovered.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness along a fixed Sobolev field from equality of all localized bulk energies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(u\in W^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\). children.title: Recession-Density Identification
children.top_down_role: Localization of densities associated with singular growth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and structural properties of the recession function for a finite convex integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(z\mapsto f(x,z)\) is finite and convex, then for every \(z_0,z\) the quotient \[t\mapsto\frac{f(x,z_0+tz)-f(x,z_0)}{t}\] is nondecreasing on \((0,\infty)\). Its limit as \(t\to\infty\) is independent of \(z_0\) and defines \(f^\infty(x,z)\). The function \(f^\infty(x,\cdot)\) is convex and positively one-homogeneous; an upper linear-growth bound makes it finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity makes the recession limit base-point independent, convex, and positively homogeneous.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot)\) is finite and convex.
An upper linear-growth bound is assumed when finiteness of \(f^\infty\) is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^\infty(x,\lambda z)=\lambda f^\infty(x,z)\quad(\lambda\ge0),\qquad f^\infty(x,\cdot)\text{ is convex}.

notation.meaning: Arbitrary finite base point in the recession quotient.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Recession Function Properties

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measure-theoretic localization of an already represented singular energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mu_u^s=f^\infty(x,\theta_u(x))\,|D^su|\), where \(\theta_u=dD^su/d|D^su|\). Then for \(|D^su|\)-almost every \(x_0\), \[f^\infty(x_0,\theta_u(x_0))=\frac{d\mu_u^s}{d|D^su|}(x_0)=\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{\mu_u^s(B_r(x_0))}{|D^su|(B_r(x_0))}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The represented recession density is recovered by differentiating singular energy with respect to the total variation of the singular derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu_u^s\ll|D^su|\) with density \(f^\infty(x,\theta_u)\).
\(\theta_u=dD^su/d|D^su|\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the ordinary recession quotient for a continuous nonconvex integrand with linear growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\) by \[f(z)=|z|\bigl(2+\sin(\log(1+|z|))\bigr).\] Then \(|z|\le f(z)\le3|z|\), but for \(z=1\), \[\frac{f(tz)-f(0)}{t}=2+\sin(\log(1+t))\] has no limit as \(t\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuity and linear growth alone do not ensure existence of the ordinary recession limit for a nonconvex integrand.
assumptions_latex: f(z)=|z|\left(2+\sin(\log(1+|z|))\right)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}\text{ does not exist}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex upper-recession object used when the ordinary recession limit need not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(x\), define
\[
f^{\#}(x,z):=\limsup_{\substack{t\to+\infty\\z'\to z}}\frac{f(x,tz')}{t}.
\]
A uniform upper linear-growth bound makes \(f^{\#}(x,\cdot)\) finite. If the ordinary recession quotient converges locally uniformly with respect to directions near \(z\), then \(f^{\#}(x,z)=f^\infty(x,z)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A joint limsup in scale and direction defines an upper recession function even when a nonconvex integrand has no ordinary recession limit.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x,\cdot):\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to[0,+\infty]\) is defined.
A uniform upper linear-growth bound is assumed when finiteness is asserted.
Equality with \(f^\infty\) requires stability of the ordinary recession limit under directional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{\#}(x,z)=\limsup_{\substack{t\to+\infty\\z'\to z}}\frac{f(x,tz')}{t}.

notation.meaning: Directional perturbation in the joint limsup.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous convex linear-growth relaxation identifying the singular density by the ordinary recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) be bounded and open and let \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to[0,+\infty)\) be finite and convex, with \(c|z|\le f(z)\le C(1+|z|)\). If \(I(v)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla v)\,dx\) on \(W^{1,1}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), then its sequential strong-\(L^1\) lower-semicontinuous envelope on \(BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) is
\[
\overline I(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx+\int_\Omega f^\infty\!\left(\frac{dD^su}{d|D^su|}\right)d|D^su|,
\qquad f^\infty(z)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(tz)}t.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an autonomous convex integrand with linear growth, relaxation from W1,1 to BV evaluates the ordinary recession function on the polar of the singular derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and open.
\(f\) is finite and convex and satisfies \(c|z|\le f(z)\le C(1+|z|)\).
The envelope is taken for sequential strong \(L^1\) convergence from \(W^{1,1}\) to \(BV\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate-Domain Representation of the Convex Recession Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual representation of a closed proper convex integrand's recession density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(x\) and let \(g(z)=f(x,z)\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then
\[
g^\infty(z)=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}g^*}(z)=\sup_{p\in\operatorname{dom}g^*}\langle p,z\rangle.
\]
An upper bound \(g(z)\le C(1+|z|)\) gives \(\operatorname{dom}g^*\subset C\mathbb B\), while \(g(z)\ge c|z|-C\) gives \(c\mathbb B\subset\operatorname{dom}g^*\) and hence \(g^\infty(z)\ge c|z|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex recession density is the support function of the effective domain of the convex conjugate.
assumptions_latex: \(g=f(x,\cdot)\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The displayed growth assumptions are imposed only for their corresponding domain conclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g^\infty=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}g^*}.

notation.meaning: Convex conjugate of the fixed-x integrand.
Support function of the set C.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is open and \(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to[0,\infty)\) is convex in its second argument.
\(f\) has linear growth and sufficient continuity in \(x\) for the standard \(BV\)-relaxation formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The singular derivative contributes \(f^\infty(x,dD^su/d|D^su|)\) per unit \(|D^su|\).

notation.meaning: Recession function of the integrand in its gradient variable.
Part of the distributional derivative singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.
Polar density of the singular derivative with respect to its total variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex linear-growth relaxation on \(BV\), with the recession function identifying singular energy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\Omega\) and \(z\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\), define
\[
f^\infty(x,z):=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(x,tz)-f(x,0)}{t},
\]
whenever the stated hypotheses guarantee this limit. If \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(Du=\nabla u\,\mathcal L^d+D^su\), then the relaxed functional has singular part
\[
\int_\Omega f^\infty\!\left(x,\frac{dD^su}{d|D^su|}(x)\right)d|D^su|(x).
\]
Thus blow-up along amplitudes diverging at rate \(t\) identifies the density carried by the singular derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function, evaluated at the polar of the singular derivative, gives the relaxed energy density on the singular part.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Density Identification

children.title: Superlinear-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Growth regimes supporting reflexive-space bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint separating the reflexive superlinear route from linear-growth compactness mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(1<p<\infty\), \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) are reflexive, and their bounded sequences are weakly relatively compact. At \(p=1\), these spaces are generally nonreflexive, so boundedness alone does not provide weak sequential compactness; uniform-integrability, BV, or measure compactness hypotheses are then needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reflexive compactness route applies above linear growth and generally fails at the exponent one endpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is open.
\(1\le p<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1<p<\infty\) gives reflexive weak compactness, whereas \(p=1\) does not in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Reflexivity Threshold for Power Growth

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(F(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx\) on \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(f(x,z,\xi)\geq\alpha(|z|^p+|\xi|^p)-\beta(x)\), where \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in L^1(\Omega)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite-energy sublevel of \(F\) is bounded in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), hence weakly relatively compact.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: p-growth coercivity and reflexivity are standard direct-method facts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A coercive \(p\)-growth regime with \(p>1\), yielding reflexive Sobolev compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(c\in\mathbb R\) and every \(u\) satisfying \(F(u)\leq c\), coercive growth gives
\[
\alpha\bigl(\|u\|_{L^p}^p+\|\nabla u\|_{L^p}^p\bigr)\leq c+\|\beta\|_{L^1}.
\]
Hence the sublevel \(\{u:F(u)\leq c\}\) is bounded in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\). Since \(1<p<\infty\), this Sobolev space is reflexive, so each sequence in the sublevel has a weakly convergent subsequence. The same conclusion holds when the \(L^p\)-term is replaced by a normalization and an applicable Poincare inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercive growth of order greater than one bounds Sobolev sublevels and supplies weakly convergent subsequences through reflexivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear-Growth Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly describes the superlinear coercive regime and reflexive compactness, but no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Linear-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Growth regimes requiring BV or measure compactness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional derivative concentration explaining the need for BV or measure compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \((0,1)\), define \[u_j(x)=\min\{jx,1\}.\] Then \((u_j)\) is bounded in \(W^{1,1}(0,1)\), since \(u_j'=j\mathbf1_{(0,1/j)}\) and \(\|u_j'\|_{L^1}=1\). The derivatives are not uniformly integrable and hence are not weakly relatively compact in \(L^1(0,1)\). Viewed as measures on \([0,1]\), \[u_j'\,\mathcal L^1\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\delta_0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded amount of gradient mass can concentrate into a measure, preventing weak L1 compactness despite bounded total variation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence is bounded in W^{1,1}, but its gradients are not weakly relatively compact in L^1.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Obstructs Weak W11 Compactness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normalization Converts Linear Derivative Growth into BV Coercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Energy-to-BV boundedness after additive constants are controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(F(u)\ge \alpha |Du|(\Omega)-C\), where \(\alpha>0\), and the admissible class has prescribed mean, an appropriate prescribed trace, or an independent coercive \(L^1\) term. Then every finite sublevel of \(F\) is bounded in \(BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\). Without such normalization, derivative growth alone does not control additions of constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear derivative growth yields BV-bounded sublevels after constants are fixed or separately controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(F(u)\ge\alpha|Du|(\Omega)-C\).
A BV Poincare normalization holds, or the energy separately controls \(\|u\|_{L^1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(u)\le c\Rightarrow \|u\|_{L^1}+|Du|(\Omega)\le C_c.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Converts Linear Derivative Growth into BV Coercivity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: BV Compactness in the Linear-Growth Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness under uniform mass and total-variation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) be bounded with Lipschitz boundary. If \((u_j)\subset BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) satisfies
\[
\sup_j\bigl(\|u_j\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+|Du_j|(\Omega)\bigr)<\infty,
\]
then a subsequence and \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) satisfy \(u_j\to u\) in \(L^1\) and \(Du_j\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}Du\) as vector-valued Radon measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform mass and total variation give strong L1 compactness and weak-star compactness of derivative measures.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is bounded with Lipschitz boundary.
The sequence has uniformly bounded \(L^1\) norm and total variation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_j\to u\text{ in }L^1,\qquad Du_j\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}Du\text{ along a subsequence}.

notation.meaning: Total variation of the distributional derivative

knowledge_statements.title: BV Compactness in the Linear-Growth Regime

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and has Lipschitz boundary.
\(F\) is defined on \(W^{1,1}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and satisfies \(F(u)\geq\alpha(\|u\|_{L^1}+\|\nabla u\|_{L^1})-C\), with \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Energy-bounded sequences are bounded in \(BV\), relatively compact in \(L^1\), and have weak-star convergent derivative measures along a subsequence.

notation.meaning: Distributional derivative, regarded as a vector-valued Radon measure.
Total variation of the derivative measure on the domain.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: linear growth naturally yields BV rather than reflexive Sobolev compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear growth provides \(BV\) and measure compactness, generally not weak compactness in \(W^{1,1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(F(u_j)\leq c\), then
\[
\sup_j\bigl(\|u_j\|_{L^1(\Omega)}+|Du_j|(\Omega)\bigr)<\infty,
\]
where \(Du_j=\nabla u_j\,\mathcal L^d\) for \(u_j\in W^{1,1}\). Consequently there exist \(u\in BV(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and a subsequence such that \(u_j\to u\) in \(L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\) and \(Du_j\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}Du\) as Radon measures. Thus a direct method for linear growth normally uses the relaxed \(BV\) domain, because bounded subsets of \(W^{1,1}\) need not be weakly relatively compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear energy growth bounds total variation, so compactness occurs in BV and in derivative measures rather than through reflexivity of W1,1.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Growth Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the linear-growth leaf and correctly distinguishes BV compactness from W^{1,1} reflexivity, but it lacks a source locator.
