knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-condition count for functionals of order at least two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\ge2\), the condition \(L_{y^{(k)}}=0\) does not exhaust endpoint stationarity when lower endpoint jets are also free. Every independently free \(y^{(r)}\), \(0\le r<k\), has its distinct condition \(P_r=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order problems require the complete hierarchy of natural endpoint conditions, not only the highest momentum condition.
assumptions_latex: At least two endpoint jet components are independently free.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{y^{(k)}}=0\text{ alone does not imply endpoint stationarity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Highest-Derivative Condition Alone Is Insufficient

assumptions_latex: L\in C^2([a,b]\times\mathbb R^3)
y\in C^4([a,b])\text{ is stationary}
y\text{ and }y'\text{ are free at the endpoint under consideration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{y''}=0,\qquad L_{y'}-\frac{d}{dt}L_{y''}=0\quad\text{at each free endpoint}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order one-dimensional prototype with free endpoint value and slope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J(y)=\int_a^bL(t,y,y',y'')\,dt\), the boundary part of the first variation is \[\left[\left(L_{y'}-\frac{d}{dt}L_{y''}\right)\eta+L_{y''}\eta'\right]_a^b.\] If \(y\) and \(y'\) are independently free at an endpoint, then \(\eta\) and \(\eta'\) are arbitrary there, giving \[L_{y''}=0,\qquad L_{y'}-\frac{d}{dt}L_{y''}=0.\] A fixed endpoint jet suppresses its corresponding natural condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a second-derivative functional, free endpoint slope and value respectively force the highest momentum and the corrected lower momentum to vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Natural Conditions

children.title: Terminal-Manifold Transversality
children.top_down_role: Endpoint stationarity relative to smooth or nonsmooth terminal sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed terminal time and a smooth terminal manifold.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A constrained extremal \(\bar u\) is normal when its first-order multiplier system has a nontrivial solution \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\) with \(\lambda_0>0\), where \(\lambda_0\) multiplies the objective variation and \(\lambda\) multiplies the active subsidiary constraints. Because a homogeneous multiplier system is invariant under common positive rescaling, normality permits the normalization \(\lambda_0=1\). The resulting stationarity condition retains the objective derivative and has the form
\[DJ(\bar u)+D\mathcal G(\bar u)^*\widehat\lambda=0,\qquad \widehat\lambda=\lambda/\lambda_0,\]
with the appropriate feasibility, sign, and complementarity conditions for \(\widehat\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extremal is normal when some nontrivial multiplier system gives the objective a positive coefficient, which can then be normalized to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal Extremals

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A constrained extremal \(\bar u\) is abnormal when a valid nontrivial first-order multiplier tuple satisfies \(\lambda_0=0\), so necessarily \(\lambda\ne0\). Its stationarity relation consequently reduces to
\[D\mathcal G(\bar u)^*\lambda=0,\]
with any required multiplier signs and complementarity relations, and contains no objective derivative. If every nontrivial multiplier tuple has \(\lambda_0=0\), the extremal is strictly abnormal; if both normal and abnormal tuples exist, the extremal remains normal under the existential convention for normality. Abnormality typically signals degeneracy of the active constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abnormal multiplier system has zero objective coefficient and a nonzero constraint multiplier, so stationarity may contain no information about the objective.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\subset[0,\infty)\times Y^*\) be positively homogeneous. A nonzero tuple \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\in M\) can be positively rescaled to an admissible tuple having objective coefficient one if and only if \(\lambda_0>0\). Thus normalization fails for every admissible nonzero tuple exactly when
\[M\cap\bigl((0,\infty)\times Y^*\bigr)=\varnothing.\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete degeneracy showing why the objective multiplier cannot always be normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The feasible set of \(G(x)=x^2=0\) is the singleton \(\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a local minimizer of \(J(x)=x\). A Fritz John multiplier pair \((\lambda_0,\mu)\ne(0,0)\), with \(\lambda_0\ge0\), must satisfy
\[0=\lambda_0J'(0)+\mu G'(0)=\lambda_0.\]
Hence every admissible nontrivial pair has \(\lambda_0=0\) and \(\mu\ne0\). No common rescaling can produce \(\lambda_0=1\). The failure is caused by the vanished constraint derivative \(G'(0)=0\), which violates the usual equality-constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For minimizing x subject to x squared equaling zero, every nontrivial Fritz John multiplier is abnormal, so objective-multiplier normalization fails.

children.title: Autonomous Integrands

assumptions_latex: \(L:[a,b]\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is an integrand.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomy with respect to the independent variable in a first-order integral functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The integrand \(L\) is autonomous when it has no explicit dependence on the independent variable: there exists a function \(\ell\) such that
\[L(t,z,v)=\ell(z,v)\qquad\text{for all }(t,z,v)\in[a,b]\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m.\]
Equivalently, if \(L\) is differentiable in \(t\), autonomy is the identity \(L_t(t,z,v)=0\) throughout its domain. Dependence through the trajectory values \(z=u(t)\) and \(v=u'(t)\) does not violate autonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrand is autonomous when it depends on the state and velocity but not explicitly on the independent variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Autonomous Integrands

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of autonomy is precise, internally consistent, and correctly classified as a definition, but no cited source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth vector-valued Beltrami identity for autonomous first-order integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(u\) be a smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal of \(I(u)=\int_a^bL(u(t),u'(t))\,dt\). Since autonomy gives \(L_t=0\), the Du Bois–Reymond identity implies
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L(u(t),u'(t))-u'(t)\cdot L_v(u(t),u'(t))\right]=0.\]
Consequently, on each connected interval of definition there exists \(C\in\mathbb R\) such that \(L-u'\cdot L_v=C\). The sign-reversed quantity \(u'\cdot L_v-L\) is an equivalent conserved Hamiltonian convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an autonomous smooth integrand, the Beltrami energy expression is constant along every smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal.
knowledge_statements.title: Beltrami First Integrals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Beltrami first-integral theorem is mathematically consistent with the stated smooth autonomous setting and fits the leaf, but it lacks a cited source and specific locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit base-variable dependence replaces Beltrami conservation by the Du Bois–Reymond source balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=L(t,z,v)\) be continuously differentiable in \(t\) and sufficiently smooth in \((z,v)\), and let \(u\in C^2\) satisfy
\[\frac{d}{dt}L_v(t,u,u')=L_z(t,u,u').\]
Then along \(u\),
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L(t,u,u')-u'\cdot L_v(t,u,u')\right]=L_t(t,u,u').\]
Thus the Beltrami expression is constant on an interval exactly when its source \(L_t(t,u(t),u'(t))\) vanishes there; global autonomy is sufficient but not necessary for this trajectorywise vanishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonautonomous integrand, the derivative of the Beltrami quantity equals the explicit-time derivative of the integrand, so conservation survives only when that source vanishes along the extremal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit time dependence destroys Beltrami conservation through the Du Bois–Reymond source term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(L(t,z,v)=\frac12v^2+t\), the Euler–Lagrange equation is \(u''=0\), so every extremal has \(u'(t)=c\) for some constant \(c\). Along such an extremal,
\[L(t,u,u')-u'L_v(t,u,u')=t-\frac12c^2,\]
and hence
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(L-u'L_v\right)=1=L_t.\]
Therefore the Beltrami expression is not conserved. This example isolates the boundary of the autonomous result: once \(L_t\ne0\), the correct statement is a balance law with source \(L_t\), not a first integral.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual identity underlying the one-dimensional first Noether theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set p=L_v, E(L)=L_z-D_tL_v, Q=\xi-u'\tau, and X=\tau\partial_t+\xi\cdot\partial_z. Then
\[\operatorname{pr}^{(1)}X(L)+L D_t\tau=Q\cdot E(L)+D_t\!\left[p\cdot\xi+(L-p\cdot u')\tau\right].\]
If the left side is D_tB, then
\[D_t\!\left[p\cdot\xi+(L-p\cdot u')\tau-B\right]=-Q\cdot E(L),\]
so the bracket is conserved on Euler–Lagrange extremals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infinitesimal density change splits into an Euler–Lagrange residual and the total derivative of the Noether current.
assumptions_latex: L, \tau, and \xi are sufficiently smooth for the displayed total derivatives.
X generates a one-parameter point transformation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional first Noether theorem with a gauge term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the infinitesimal transformation \(t\mapsto t+\varepsilon\tau(t,z)\), \(z\mapsto z+\varepsilon\xi(t,z)\) changes the density \(L(t,u,u')\,dt\), to first order in \(\varepsilon\), only by \(\frac{d}{dt}B(t,u(t))\,dt\). Then every smooth Euler–Lagrange extremal satisfies
\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[L_v(t,u,u')\cdot\xi(t,u)+\left(L(t,u,u')-u'\cdot L_v(t,u,u')\right)\tau(t,u)-B(t,u)\right]=0.\]
Thus each continuous variational symmetry yields a conserved quantity; time translations and state translations recover energy and momentum families, respectively.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

For every \(\eta\in C_c^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^n)\), stationarity under the inner variation generated by \(x\mapsto x+\varepsilon\eta(x)\) gives
\[\int_\Omega\left[F(u,Du)\operatorname{div}\eta-F_P(u,Du):(Du\,D\eta)\right]dx=0.\]

\[\int_\Omega T:D\eta\,dx=0,\qquad\operatorname{div}T=0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(\Omega;\mathbb R^n).\]

For a continuous junction of two arcs with one-sided velocities \(v^-\) and \(v^+\), the linearized movable-junction geometry is
\[
\mathcal J:=\left\{(\sigma,\eta^-,\eta^+):

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Minimizer with No Classical Euler Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly convex variational problem whose Sobolev minimizer satisfies the Euler equation weakly but is not twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(t)=1\) on \((0,1/2)\) and \(g(t)=-1\) on \((1/2,1)\), and minimize \[J(u)=\int_0^1\left(\frac12|u'(t)|^2-g(t)u(t)\right)dt\] over \(H_0^1(0,1)\). The unique minimizer \(\bar u\) satisfies \[\int_0^1\bar u'(t)v'(t)\,dt=\int_0^1g(t)v(t)\,dt\qquad(v\in H_0^1(0,1)),\] equivalently \(-\bar u''=g\) distributionally and almost everywhere. Its second derivative jumps at \(t=1/2\), so \(\bar u\notin C^2([0,1])\) and the equation is not classical throughout \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discontinuous forcing produces a Sobolev minimizer satisfying the Euler equation weakly but not as a classical equation at every interior point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite measure space, set \(q_h=[f(h,\cdot)-f(0,\cdot)]/h\). If \(q_h\to q\) in measure and \(\{q_h:0<|h|<h_0\}\) is uniformly integrable, then \(q_h\to q\) in \(L^1\) and \[\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\int_T f(h,t)\,d\mu-\int_T f(0,t)\,d\mu}{h}=\int_Tq(t)\,d\mu(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence in measure of the difference quotients permits differentiation under the integral when those quotients are uniformly integrable.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu(T)<\infty\).
\(q_h\to q\) in measure as \(h\to0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary one-sided counterexample driven by non-uniformly-integrable difference quotients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\varepsilon\ge0\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), let \(f(0,t)=0\) and \(f(\varepsilon,t)=\mathbf 1_{(0,\varepsilon)}(t)\). For every fixed \(t>0\), \(\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)=0\), but \[I(\varepsilon)=\int_0^1f(\varepsilon,t)\,dt=\varepsilon\quad(0\le\varepsilon\le1),\qquad I'(0^+)=1.\] The quotients \(\varepsilon^{-1}\mathbf 1_{(0,\varepsilon)}\) concentrate at zero and are not uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shrinking moving interval has zero pointwise right derivative but an integral with right derivative one.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le\varepsilon\le1\) and the integration domain is \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I'(0^+)=1\ne0=\int_0^1\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)\,dt\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integrable-domination regime preventing concentration of parameter derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)\times T\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in \(t\), differentiable in \(\varepsilon\) for almost every \(t\), and suppose \(f(0,\cdot)\in L^1(\mu)\). If some \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) satisfies \(|\partial_\varepsilon f(\varepsilon,t)|\le g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and all \(|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0\), then \[\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int_Tf(\varepsilon,t)\,d\mu(t)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\int_T\partial_\varepsilon f(0,t)\,d\mu(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable bound on the parameter derivative justifies differentiation under the integral sign.
assumptions_latex: \(f(\cdot,t)\) is differentiable for almost every \(t\).
\(|\partial_\varepsilon f(\varepsilon,t)|\le g(t)\) for some \(g\in L^1(\mu)\).

assumptions_latex: The parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\) and the integration domain is \((0,1)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete concentration counterexample to unqualified differentiation under the integral sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(f(0,t)=0\) and, for \(\varepsilon>0\), \(f(\varepsilon,t)=\varepsilon^2/(t+\varepsilon)^2\) on \((0,1)\). For every fixed \(t>0\),
\[
\partial_\varepsilon f(0^+,t)=0.
\]
Nevertheless,
\[
I(\varepsilon):=\int_0^1 f(\varepsilon,t)\,dt=\frac{\varepsilon}{1+\varepsilon},
\qquad I'(0^+)=1.
\]
Hence differentiation and integration do not commute because the difference quotients lack a common integrable dominating function near \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise parameter derivatives vanish, but concentration near the integration boundary makes the derivative of the integral equal one.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Differentiation Under Integration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent and limiting-normal description of a closed nonsmooth feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bouligand tangent cone and limiting normal cone of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) are
\[
T_C(\bar x):=\left\{d:\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ x_k\in C,\ x_k\to\bar x,\frac{x_k-\bar x}{t_k}\to d\right\},
\]
\[
N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v:\exists x_k\to_C\bar x,\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Unlike smooth constraint geometry, these cones may be nonconvex and need not be linear subspaces or mutual polars.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth feasibility is modeled by contingent directions and limiting normals, which may be nonconvex and need not form complementary subspaces.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Constraint Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone regularity criterion at a nonsmooth feasible boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A closed set \(C\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\in C\) when its regular and limiting normal cones coincide:
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x).
\]
Equivalently, every limiting normal at \(\bar x\) already satisfies the first-order regular-normal inequality there. Failure of this equality identifies boundary points where nearby normal directions create additional limiting normals and smooth-style first-order geometry is unreliable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar failure of coderivative stationarity when metric subregularity is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(x)=\{x^2\}\) and minimize \(f(x)=x\) subject to \(0\in G(x)\). The feasible set is \(S=\{0\}\), so \(\bar x=0\) is a constrained local minimizer. However \[D^*G(0,0)(y^*)=\{0\}\quad\text{for every }y^*\in\mathbb R,\] and hence \(0\notin\partial f(0)+D^*G(0,0)(y^*)=\{1\}\). Metric subregularity fails because \(|x|\le\kappa x^2\) cannot hold near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degenerate squaring constraint has a singleton feasible set but no coderivative multiplier balancing a nonzero objective gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\) is a constrained minimizer, but coderivative stationarity fails for every multiplier.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) have locally closed graph at \((\bar x,0)\), put \(S=G^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(G\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,0)\): \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,G(x))\quad\text{near }\bar x.\] If a locally Lipschitz function \(f\) has a local minimum over \(S\) at \(\bar x\), then there exist \(x^*\in\partial f(\bar x)\) and \(y^*\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \[-x^*\in D^*G(\bar x,0)(y^*).\]

For the generalized-equation constraint \(0\in G(x)\), suppose an applicable inverse-image normal-cone qualification gives

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(W_0^{1,4}(0,1)\), define \[J[y]=-\int_0^1|y'(t)|^4\,dt.\] At \(\bar y=0\), \(DJ(0)=0\) and \(D^2J(0)[h,h]=0\ge0\) for every fixed-endpoint variation \(h\). Nevertheless, \(J[\varepsilon h]<J[0]\) for every nonzero \(h\) and every \(\varepsilon\ne0\). Thus stationarity and nonnegative second variation do not imply fixed-endpoint local minimality without stricter curvature or higher-order control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary fixed-endpoint arc can have identically zero second variation and still fail to be a local minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=H_0^1(a,b;\mathbb R^n)\), and suppose \(J\) is twice Fréchet differentiable near a stationary arc \(\bar y\) in \(\bar y+X\). If some \(c>0\) satisfies \[D^2J(\bar y)[h,h]\ge c\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}^2\qquad(h\in X),\] then for every \(\gamma\in(0,c/2)\) there is \(\rho>0\) such that \[J(\bar y+h)\ge J(\bar y)+\gamma\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}^2\] whenever \(h\in X\) and \(\lVert h\rVert_{H^1}<\rho\). Hence \(\bar y\) is an isolated strict fixed-endpoint local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform coercivity of the fixed-endpoint second variation yields local quadratic growth and isolated strict minimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical quadratic second variation and its necessary nonnegativity condition for fixed endpoint data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b L(t,y(t),\dot y(t))\,dt\). For a fixed-endpoint variation \(\eta\in C^1([a,b];\mathbb R^n)\) with \(\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0\), the second variation is
\[
\delta^2J[y](\eta)=\int_a^b\left(\eta^{\mathsf T}L_{yy}\eta+2\eta^{\mathsf T}L_{yv}\dot\eta+\dot\eta^{\mathsf T}L_{vv}\dot\eta\right)\,dt,
\]
where all derivatives of \(L\) are evaluated at \((t,y(t),\dot y(t))\). If \(y\) is a weak local minimizer, then \(\delta^2J[y](\eta)\ge 0\) for every such fixed-endpoint variation \(\eta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar y\) be a constrained local minimizer and let \(\lambda\) satisfy the corresponding first-order multiplier system. For every critical variation \(h\in K(\bar y,\lambda)\), second-order necessity requires
\[
D^2_{yy}\mathcal L(\bar y,\lambda)[h,h]\ge0.
\]
The cone \(K(\bar y,\lambda)\) consists of directions satisfying the linearized equality constraints, the appropriate tangent conditions for active inequalities, and zero first-order Lagrangian-compatible objective decrease. Thus positivity is required on the critical cone, not on the entire ambient variation space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a constrained minimum, the Lagrangian’s second derivative must be nonnegative on variations that are both linearly feasible and first-order critical.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every admissible variation \(v\), the second variation is
\[
Q_u[v]=\int_\Omega\!\left[v^{\mathsf T}F_{zz}v+2v^{\mathsf T}F_{zP}:\nabla v+\nabla v:F_{PP}:\nabla v\right]_{(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))}\,dx.
\]

children.title: Weak Legendre Condition
children.top_down_role: Classical nonnegative second-order gradient geometry for weak extrema.

assumptions_latex: \(F(t,y,p)\) is twice continuously differentiable in \(p\).
\(\bar y\) is a weak local minimizer of \(\int_a^b F(t,y,y')\,dt\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\xi^{\mathsf T}F_{pp}(t,\bar y(t),\bar y'(t))\xi\ge0\) for every \(\xi\).

notation.meaning: Hessian with respect to the derivative variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Legendre necessary condition for a smooth weak minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The weak Legendre condition along \(\bar y\) is
\[
\xi^{\mathsf T}F_{pp}(t,\bar y(t),\bar y'(t))\xi\ge 0
\quad\text{for every }\xi\in\mathbb R^m
\]
for every \(t\in[a,b]\) at which the coefficients are defined. Thus the derivative-variable Hessian is positive semidefinite along the extremal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth weak minimum, the integrand's Hessian in the derivative variable must be positive semidefinite along the extremal.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Legendre Condition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind and positive-semidefinite conclusion fit the Weak Legendre Condition leaf. A source is required to establish the precise weak-minimum topology, coefficient regularity, and pointwise domain on which the necessary condition holds.

children.title: Strengthened Legendre Condition
children.top_down_role: Uniformly positive second-order gradient geometry.

assumptions_latex: \(F\in C^2\) near the graph of \((\bar y,\bar y')\).
\([a,b]\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{pp}(t,\bar y(t),\bar y'(t))\succeq\alpha I\) uniformly for some \(\alpha>0\).

notation.meaning: Derivative-variable Hessian along the reference arc
Identity matrix on the derivative space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform positive-definiteness version of the classical Legendre condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The strengthened Legendre condition holds when there exists a constant \(\alpha>0\) such that
\[
\xi^{\mathsf T}P(t)\xi\ge\alpha\lVert\xi\rVert^2
\quad\text{for all }t\in[a,b]\text{ and }\xi\in\mathbb R^m.
\]
Equivalently, the smallest eigenvalue of \(P(t)\) is bounded below by one positive constant throughout the interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative-variable Hessian is uniformly positive definite along the reference extremal, with one positive lower bound valid everywhere.
knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Legendre Condition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform positive-definiteness condition and condition content kind fit the strengthened Legendre leaf. No source supports the stated convention or the equivalence with a uniform eigenvalue bound along the reference arc.

children.title: Legendre–Hadamard Condition
children.top_down_role: Rank-one second-order geometry for vectorial multiple integrals.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acoustic-Tensor Form of the Legendre–Hadamard Condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent pointwise representation of rank-one nonnegativity and its uniform strengthening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_{\alpha i\beta j}=\partial^2F/\partial P_{\alpha i}\partial P_{\beta j}\) at a fixed \((x,z,P)\), and define \(Q(b)_{\alpha\beta}=A_{\alpha i\beta j}b_i b_j\). Then \[D^2_{PP}F[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]=a^{\mathsf T}Q(b)a.\] Hence the Legendre–Hadamard condition is equivalent to \(Q(b)\succeq0\) for every \(b\). Its strengthened form requires a constant \(c>0\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}Q(b)a\ge c\lVert a\rVert^2\lVert b\rVert^2\) for all \(a,b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank-one nonnegativity is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of every acoustic tensor; a uniform rank-one lower bound is its strengthened form.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is twice differentiable in the matrix variable \(P\).
The Hessian coefficients are evaluated at a fixed state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^2_{PP}F[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]\ge0\ \forall a,b\iff Q(b)\succeq0\ \forall b.
knowledge_statements.title: Acoustic-Tensor Form of the Legendre–Hadamard Condition

assumptions_latex: \(F(x,z,P)\in C^2\) in the matrix variable \(P\).
\(u:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m\) is a smooth weak local minimizer of the multiple integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^2_{PP}F(x,u,\nabla u)[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Second derivative in the matrix-gradient variable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one necessary condition for smooth vectorial multiple integrals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Legendre–Hadamard condition along \(u\) is
\[
D^2_{PP}F(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))[a\otimes b,a\otimes b]\ge0
\]
for every \(a\in\mathbb R^m\), \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(x\in\Omega\). It tests the gradient Hessian only on rank-one matrices, the directions generated locally by oscillatory gradient variations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vectorial multiple integral, the gradient Hessian must be nonnegative on every rank-one matrix direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Legendre–Hadamard Condition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-one inequality and condition content kind match the Legendre-Hadamard container. An authoritative locator is needed because the exact necessary condition depends on the chosen local-minimum topology, admissible variations, and regularity of the multiple integral.

children.title: Legendre-Condition Scope Limits
children.top_down_role: Insufficiency of pointwise second-order positivity for minimality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict Legendre positivity does not imply nonnegative second variation or local minimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-endpoint example separating pointwise gradient positivity from minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
I[y]=\int_0^1\bigl((y')^2-\lambda y^2\bigr)\,dt,
\]
the zero arc is stationary and \(F_{pp}=2>0\), so the strengthened Legendre condition holds. Nevertheless, with \(v(t)=\sin(\pi t)\),
\[
\delta^2I(0)[v,v]=2\int_0^1\bigl((v')^2-\lambda v^2\bigr)\,dt=\pi^2-\lambda<0.
\]
Hence pointwise positivity in the derivative variable alone is insufficient for minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional can have a uniformly positive derivative Hessian yet possess a negative second-variation direction because of its field-variable term.
knowledge_statements.title: Legendre-Condition Scope Limits

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample content kind is appropriate for the scope-limits leaf, and the displayed test direction gives the stated negative value while the derivative Hessian remains strictly positive. The record nevertheless has no cited source or inspectable locator for this classical failure example.

children.title: Jacobi Equation Family
children.top_down_role: Linearized-extremal equation families arising from second variation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hamiltonian representation for an invertible strengthened-Legendre block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(p=P\eta'+R\eta\). If \(P\) is invertible, the Jacobi equation is equivalent to \[ \frac d{dt}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\p\end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix} -P^{-1}R & P^{-1}\\ Q-R^{\mathsf T}P^{-1}R & R^{\mathsf T}P^{-1} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\p\end{pmatrix}. \] The coefficient matrix is Hamiltonian. Hence its fundamental matrix \(\Phi(t,s)\) is symplectic, and \[ \eta_1^{\mathsf T}p_2-p_1^{\mathsf T}\eta_2 \] is constant for every pair of Jacobi solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible leading block converts the Jacobi equation into a Hamiltonian system with symplectic flow and conserved Wronskian.
assumptions_latex: \(P=P^{\mathsf T}\) is pointwise invertible and \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\).
The coefficients admit a fundamental evolution matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Jacobi flow is symplectic and preserves the Jacobi boundary concomitant.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Hamiltonian Jacobi System

assumptions_latex: \(F(t,y,p)\in C^2\) and \(\bar y\) is a smooth extremal.
\(P=F_{pp}\), \(R=F_{py}\), and \(Q=F_{yy}\) are evaluated along \((\bar y,\bar y')\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Jacobi fields are precisely solutions of \(-\frac d{dt}(P\eta'+R\eta)+R^{\mathsf T}\eta'+Q\eta=0\).

notation.meaning: Derivative, mixed, and state Hessian blocks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix Jacobi equation for vector-valued one-dimensional variational problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quadratic second-variation integrand is
\[
\eta'^{\mathsf T}P\eta'+2\eta'^{\mathsf T}R\eta+\eta^{\mathsf T}Q\eta.
\]
Its Euler equation, called the Jacobi equation, is
\[
-\frac d{dt}\bigl(P\eta'+R\eta\bigr)+R^{\mathsf T}\eta'+Q\eta=0.
\]
Varying the initial data produces the Jacobi equation family; equivalently, its members are linearizations of smooth one-parameter families of Euler–Lagrange extremals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearizing the Euler–Lagrange equation yields a matrix second-order Jacobi equation whose solutions are Jacobi fields.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi Equation Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed Euler equation is consistent with the stated quadratic integrand, and representation is suitable for the Jacobi-equation-family leaf. A source is required for the stronger claim that its solutions are equivalently linearizations of smooth one-parameter families of extremals, especially without an explicit regularity or nondegeneracy assumption on the leading block.

children.title: Conjugate-Focal Point Geometry

children.title: Conjugate Points
children.top_down_role: Second-order obstructions associated primarily with fixed-endpoint geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular fixed-endpoint Jacobi systems under strengthened Legendre positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a regular \(m\)-dimensional Jacobi system with \(P(t)\succ0\), conjugate instants to \(a\) are isolated in \((a,b]\), and every conjugate instant has multiplicity at most \(m\). Consequently, each \([a+\varepsilon,b]\), \(\varepsilon>0\), contains only finitely many conjugate instants counted with multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a regular positive-definite Jacobi system, conjugate points are isolated and have finite multiplicity.
assumptions_latex: The state dimension is finite.
The coefficients give a regular Jacobi system and \(P(t)\succ0\) on \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Conjugate instants are isolated and have multiplicity at most \(m\).
knowledge_statements.title: Isolation and Finite Multiplicity

assumptions_latex: The Jacobi equation is regular on \([a,b]\).
Both endpoints are fixed, so admissible Jacobi fields satisfy homogeneous endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is conjugate to \(a\) exactly when a nonzero Jacobi field vanishes at both \(a\) and \(c\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical fixed-endpoint definition relative to the left endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(c\in(a,b]\) is conjugate to \(a\) along the reference extremal if there exists a Jacobi field \(\eta\not\equiv0\) on \([a,c]\) satisfying
\[
\eta(a)=0,
\qquad
\eta(c)=0.
\]
Its multiplicity is the dimension of the vector space of Jacobi fields satisfying these two boundary conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is conjugate to the initial endpoint when a nonzero Jacobi field vanishes at both points.
knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Points

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind and two-point vanishing criterion fit the fixed-endpoint sense of Conjugate Points. No authoritative source with a definition or page locator is supplied for the convention and multiplicity statement.

children.title: Focal Points
children.top_down_role: Second-order obstructions associated with variable or constrained endpoint geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-independent representation after the linearized endpoint conditions have been fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal J_M\) be the finite-dimensional space of Jacobi fields satisfying the prescribed linearized admissibility and transversality conditions at the endpoint manifold \(M\). Define \(E_c:\mathcal J_M\to\mathbb R^m\) by \(E_c\eta=\eta(c)\). Then \[ c\text{ is focal to }M\iff\ker E_c\ne\{0\},\qquad \operatorname{mult}_M(c)=\dim\ker E_c. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Focality is loss of injectivity of terminal evaluation on Jacobi fields satisfying the manifold endpoint conditions.
assumptions_latex: A fixed linearized endpoint convention determines the Jacobi-field space \(\mathcal J_M\).
Jacobi evolution is regular up to \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Focal multiplicity equals \(\dim\ker E_c\).

notation.meaning: Jacobi fields satisfying the initial manifold conditions
Evaluation at the candidate focal instant

knowledge_statements.title: Focal Multiplicity as Evaluation-Map Nullity

assumptions_latex: The initial endpoint lies on a smooth constraint manifold \(M\).
Jacobi fields satisfy the linearized transversality condition at the initial endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is focal to \(M\) exactly when a nonzero admissible Jacobi field satisfies \(\eta(c)=0\).

notation.meaning: Jacobi field satisfying initial linearized endpoint conditions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-initial-endpoint focality relative to a smooth endpoint manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(c\in(a,b]\) is focal to \(M\) along the reference extremal if there exists a nonzero Jacobi field \(\eta\) such that
\[
\eta(a)\in T_{\bar y(a)}M,
\qquad
\eta(c)=0,
\]
and \(\eta\) satisfies the linearized natural transversality condition at \(a\). The focal multiplicity is the dimension of the space of such fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A focal point occurs when a nonzero Jacobi field allowed by the initial endpoint constraint vanishes later along the extremal.
knowledge_statements.title: Focal Points

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct content kind for Focal Points, but the linearized natural transversality condition is not stated explicitly. Its form can depend on the endpoint manifold, boundary term, momentum convention, and second fundamental form, so the mathematical definition cannot be validated without a specific source.

children.title: Fixed-Endpoint Point Geometry
children.top_down_role: Point configurations arising under fixed terminal data.

assumptions_latex: \(Y(t)\) is a fundamental matrix of Jacobi fields with \(Y(a)=0\).
The initial momentum normalization of \(Y\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c\) is conjugate to \(a\) if and only if \(\det Y(c)=0\).

notation.meaning: Fundamental matrix of initially vanishing Jacobi fields

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fundamental-matrix geometry for fixed endpoint conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed endpoints, the Jacobi fields satisfying \(\eta(a)=0\) are represented by
\[
\eta(t)=Y(t)c,
\qquad c\in\mathbb R^m.
\]
A point \(t=c_0\) is conjugate to \(a\) precisely when the evaluation map loses injectivity, equivalently
\[
\ker Y(c_0)\ne\{0\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\det Y(c_0)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed endpoints, conjugate points are exactly the locations where the fundamental matrix of initially vanishing Jacobi fields becomes singular.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Endpoint Point Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fundamental-matrix representation fits the Fixed-Endpoint Point Geometry leaf, and singularity of the evaluation matrix is the expected conjugacy criterion under a valid normalization. A source is needed to specify the regular Jacobi system, matrix dimension, and initial momentum normalization that make the representation complete.

children.title: Variable-Endpoint Point Geometry
children.top_down_role: Point configurations shaped by movable terminal data or endpoint manifolds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symplectic Criterion for Self-Adjoint Endpoint Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural criterion for linearized endpoint subspaces in Jacobi Cauchy-data space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Jacobi Cauchy data \(z=(\eta,p)\), where \(p=P\eta'+R\eta\), define \[ \omega(z_1,z_2)=\eta_1^{\mathsf T}p_2-p_1^{\mathsf T}\eta_2. \] Jacobi evolution preserves \(\omega\). A linear endpoint-data subspace \(L\subset\mathbb R^{2m}\) annihilates the integration-by-parts boundary form exactly when \(\omega|_{L\times L}=0\). A maximal such \(m\)-dimensional subspace is Lagrangian and supplies self-adjoint separated endpoint data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Self-adjoint linear endpoint conditions correspond to Lagrangian subspaces of Jacobi Cauchy-data space.
assumptions_latex: The Jacobi equation is regular and uses momentum \(p=P\eta'+R\eta\).
Endpoint conditions have been linearized into Cauchy-data subspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximal endpoint subspaces annihilating the Jacobi boundary form are Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.title: Symplectic Criterion for Self-Adjoint Endpoint Data

assumptions_latex: Admissible endpoint variations define linear boundary subspaces \(L_a\) and \(L_c\) in Jacobi Cauchy-data space.
Jacobi evolution from \(a\) to \(c\) is the linear map \(\Phi_{c,a}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Endpoint degeneracy occurs exactly when \(\Phi_{c,a}(L_a)\cap L_c\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary-subspace formulation covering variable endpoint constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nontrivial Jacobi field satisfies the linearized variable-endpoint conditions at \(a\) and \(c\) exactly when its initial Cauchy datum lies in \(L_a\) and its evolved datum lies in \(L_c\). Consequently, endpoint degeneracy is characterized by
\[
\Phi_{c,a}(L_a)\cap L_c\ne\{0\}.
\]
For a fixed terminal endpoint this reduces to vanishing of the field component; for a free endpoint it includes the linearized natural boundary condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-endpoint focality is an intersection of the evolved admissible initial boundary data with the admissible terminal boundary data.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Endpoint Point Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary-data intersection representation fits the variable-endpoint geometry leaf. The spaces containing the Cauchy data, the transport identification, and the precise endpoint boundary subspaces are not defined sufficiently to validate the intersection formula or its fixed/free endpoint reductions without a source.

children.title: Accessory Variational Problems
children.top_down_role: Quadratic auxiliary problems organizing Jacobi theory.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar completion-of-squares certificate for the accessory index form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[ I[h]=\int_a^b(Ph'^2+2Rhh'+Qh^2)dt, \] let \(u\) be a nowhere-zero solution of \[ -(Pu'+Ru)'+Ru'+Qu=0. \] Then \[ Ph'^2+2Rhh'+Qh^2=Pu^2\left(\frac hu\right)'^2+\frac d{dt}\left(\frac{Pu'+Ru}{u}h^2\right). \] If \(h(a)=h(b)=0\) and \(P>0\), then \[ I[h]=\int_a^bPu^2\left(\frac hu\right)'^2dt\ge0. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonvanishing scalar Jacobi solution converts the index form into a square plus an endpoint term.
assumptions_latex: The problem is scalar, \(P>0\), and all quantities have the stated differentiability.
\(u\) solves the Jacobi equation and has no zero on \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For fixed-zero endpoint variations, \(I[h]\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Jacobi–Picone Completion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric bilinear representation of the accessory quadratic functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=P^{\mathsf T}\), \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), and define \[ I(\eta,\zeta)=\int_a^b\left(\eta'^{\mathsf T}P\zeta'+\eta'^{\mathsf T}R\zeta+\eta^{\mathsf T}R^{\mathsf T}\zeta'+\eta^{\mathsf T}Q\zeta\right)dt. \] Then \(I\) is symmetric, \(\mathcal A[\eta]=\tfrac12I(\eta,\eta)\), and, when the endpoint conditions annihilate the boundary concomitant, \[ I(\eta,\zeta)=\int_a^b\eta^{\mathsf T}\left[-\frac d{dt}(P\zeta'+R\zeta)+R^{\mathsf T}\zeta'+Q\zeta\right]dt. \]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The accessory functional is the diagonal of a symmetric index form representing the Jacobi operator.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\) are symmetric and the coefficients permit integration by parts.
The homogeneous endpoint conditions annihilate the boundary concomitant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A[\eta]=\tfrac12I(\eta,\eta)\), and \(I\) represents the Jacobi operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Polarized Index Form

assumptions_latex: \(P(t)=P(t)^{\mathsf T}\), \(Q(t)=Q(t)^{\mathsf T}\), and the coefficients are continuous.
Variations satisfy the prescribed homogeneous linear endpoint conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euler equation of the accessory functional is the Jacobi equation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic functional whose Euler equation organizes Jacobi theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The accessory variational problem is the quadratic problem
\[
\mathcal A[\eta]=\frac12\int_a^b\left(\eta'^{\mathsf T}P\eta'+2\eta'^{\mathsf T}R\eta+\eta^{\mathsf T}Q\eta\right)dt
\]
subject to the linearized endpoint conditions. Its Euler equation is
\[
-\frac d{dt}(P\eta'+R\eta)+R^{\mathsf T}\eta'+Q\eta=0,
\]
so its stationary fields are precisely the admissible Jacobi fields.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The accessory problem minimizes or studies the quadratic second-variation functional; its stationary fields solve the Jacobi equation.
knowledge_statements.title: Accessory Variational Problems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition content kind is appropriate for the accessory variational problem, and the formal Euler equation matches the displayed quadratic functional. A source is required for the admissible function space, endpoint conditions, coefficient regularity, and the assertion that stationary fields are precisely the admissible Jacobi fields.

children.title: Jacobi Optimality Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: Minimality regimes distinguished by conjugate-point geometry and endpoint conditions.

children.title: Jacobi Necessary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conjugate-point configurations relevant to necessary minimality tests.

assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\) is a weak local minimizer with fixed endpoints.
The second variation is regular and \(P(t)=F_{pp}(t,\bar y,\bar y')\) is positive definite on \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No point \(c\in(a,b)\) is conjugate to \(a\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical fixed-endpoint Jacobi necessary condition under regular Legendre positivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\bar y\) is a weak local minimizer and the regular Legendre condition holds, then there is no nonzero Jacobi field \(\eta\) satisfying
\[
\eta(a)=0,
\qquad
\eta(c)=0
\]
for any \(c\in(a,b)\). Thus the open interval contains no point conjugate to \(a\). Conjugacy at \(b\) is a borderline degeneracy and is not excluded by this necessary statement alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular fixed-endpoint weak minimum cannot contain an interior point conjugate to the initial endpoint; terminal conjugacy remains a borderline case.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi Necessary Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem content kind fits Jacobi Necessary Regimes, and the statement appropriately distinguishes interior conjugacy from terminal degeneracy. A specific authoritative theorem locator is needed to confirm the required regularity, strengthened Legendre hypothesis, admissible topology, and endpoint convention.

children.title: Jacobi Sufficient Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conjugate-point configurations supporting sufficient minimality certificates.

assumptions_latex: \(L\in C^2\) near the graph of a scalar extremal \(\bar y\) on \([a,b]\).
The endpoints are fixed and \(P(t):=L_{vv}(t,\bar y(t),\bar y'(t))>0\) on \([a,b]\).
No point of \((a,b]\) is conjugate to \(a\) for the Jacobi equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta^2J[\bar y](h)>0\) for every nonzero \(h\in H_0^1(a,b)\), and \(\bar y\) is a strict weak local minimizer.

notation.meaning: second variation of the integral functional

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar, regular, fixed-endpoint Jacobi sufficiency with the strengthened Legendre condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^b L(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt\), and let \(\bar y\) satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation. Put \(P=L_{vv}[\bar y]\) and \(Q=L_{yy}[\bar y]-\frac{d}{dt}L_{yv}[\bar y]\). A point \(c\in(a,b]\) is conjugate to \(a\) when \(-(Pu')'+Qu=0\) has a nonzero solution with \(u(a)=u(c)=0\). If \(P>0\) and no such \(c\) exists, then \[\delta^2J[\bar y](h)=\int_a^b\bigl(P(h')^2+Qh^2\bigr)\,dt>0\] for every nonzero \(h\in H_0^1(a,b)\); consequently \(\bar y\) is a strict weak local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strengthened Legendre condition and absence of conjugate points through the terminal endpoint make the second variation positive and yield strict weak local minimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi Sufficient Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the Jacobi sufficient-regime leaf, and the scalar fixed-endpoint formulation is mathematically plausible. However, the positivity and strict weak-minimality conclusion has no cited source or inspectable locator, so its hypotheses and endpoint convention cannot be independently verified.

children.title: Endpoint-Sensitive Jacobi Regimes
children.top_down_role: Jacobi classifications whose force depends on terminal geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-coefficient model showing how terminal geometry changes the first Jacobi degeneracy threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[ I_\lambda[h]=\int_0^L(h'^2-\lambda h^2)dt, \qquad h(0)=0, \] the fixed-terminal condition \(h(L)=0\) has first degeneracy at \[ \lambda_D=\left(\frac{\pi}{L}\right)^2,\qquad h_D(t)=\sin\frac{\pi t}{L}. \] If the terminal value is free, the natural linearized condition is \(h'(L)=0\), and first degeneracy occurs at \[ \lambda_N=\left(\frac{\pi}{2L}\right)^2,\qquad h_N(t)=\sin\frac{\pi t}{2L}. \] Thus changing only the terminal boundary geometry changes both the admissible Jacobi field and the degeneracy threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same Jacobi differential equation has different first degeneracy thresholds for fixed and natural terminal conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(L>0\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\).
Variations satisfy \(h(0)=0\), together with either \(h(L)=0\) or \(h'(L)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_D=(\pi/L)^2\), whereas \(\lambda_N=(\pi/(2L))^2\).

notation.meaning: First Dirichlet and natural-boundary degeneracy thresholds

knowledge_statements.title: Dirichlet–Natural Endpoint Threshold Shift

assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\) is a scalar fixed-endpoint weak local minimizer satisfying the Euler–Lagrange equation.
\(L\in C^2\) and \(L_{vv}[\bar y]>0\) on \([a,b]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No point in \((a,b)\) is conjugate to \(a\); sufficiency requires the stronger exclusion of conjugacy on \((a,b]\).

notation.meaning: right endpoint of the variational interval

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes interior conjugacy from conjugacy exactly at the fixed terminal endpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the fixed-endpoint problem \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y,y')\,dt\), the Jacobi necessary and sufficient regimes treat \(b\) differently. Under \(L_{vv}[\bar y]>0\), weak local minimality implies that no \(c\in(a,b)\) is conjugate to \(a\). Positive-definite Jacobi sufficiency requires that no \(c\in(a,b]\) be conjugate to \(a\). Thus a first conjugate point at \(c=b\) is compatible with the necessary condition but violates the usual strict sufficient condition because a nonzero endpoint-vanishing Jacobi field can lie in the nullspace of \(\delta^2J[\bar y]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Necessary Jacobi conditions exclude interior conjugate points, while strict sufficiency also excludes conjugacy at the terminal endpoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint-Sensitive Jacobi Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Opposite Higher-Order Outcomes at the Jacobi Threshold
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar fixed-endpoint pair showing that terminal conjugacy alone is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \([0,\pi]\), with \(y(0)=y(\pi)=0\), define \[ J_{\pm}[y]=\int_0^\pi\left[\frac12(y'^2-y^2)\pm y^4\right]dt. \] At \(\bar y=0\), both have \[ \delta^2J_{\pm}(0)[h]=\int_0^\pi(h'^2-h^2)dt\ge0, \] with nullspace \(\operatorname{span}\{\sin t\}\); thus \(\pi\) is the first conjugate point to \(0\). Nevertheless, \(J_+[y]\ge0=J_+[0]\), with equality only at \(y=0\), whereas \[ J_-[\varepsilon\sin t]= -\varepsilon^4\int_0^\pi\sin^4t\,dt<0. \] Hence \(0\) is a strict minimizer for \(J_+\) but not a minimizer for \(J_-\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shrinking Support Alone Does Not Ensure Strong Closeness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Amplitude-concentration boundary for localized perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The condition \(|S_k|\to0\) alone does not imply \(\|y_k- ar y\|_\infty\to0\). The controlling quantity is the accumulated velocity perturbation \(\int_{S_k}|y_k'-\bar y'|\,dt\). Velocity amplitudes of order \(|S_k|^{-1}\) can keep this quantity, and hence the possible state displacement, of order one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shrinking support can carry a sufficiently large velocity concentration to prevent uniform convergence.
assumptions_latex: The arcs are absolutely continuous, share the initial endpoint, and their derivative difference is supported in \(S_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S_k|\to0\text{ without }\int_{S_k}|y_k'-\bar y'|\,dt\to0\text{ does not guarantee uniform closeness.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology distinction realized by localized derivative concentration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sequence may satisfy \(\|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\to0\) while \(\|y_k'-\bar y'\|_\infty\not\to0\). It therefore enters every classical strong neighborhood based on uniform state distance but need not enter weak neighborhoods that also control the derivative. Localized derivative concentrations consequently test strong minimality beyond derivative-small variations.

Then \[y_k(t)-\bar y(t)=\int_a^t w_k(s)\,ds,\qquad \|y_k-\bar y\|_\infty\le\int_{S_k}|w_k|\,dt\le |S_k|\|w_k\|_\infty.\] If the final endpoint is also fixed, \(\int_{S_k}w_k=0\) is required. Thus bounded order-one velocity deviations on shrinking intervals give uniformly vanishing state deviations without derivative-norm convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrinking support converts bounded velocity changes into uniformly small state displacements; endpoint preservation additionally requires cancellation.

If the second variation is coercive, meaning that some \(\alpha>0\) satisfies \[\delta^2J[\bar y](h)\ge\alpha\|h\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2\quad\text{for all }h\in H_0^1(a,b),\] then there exist \(c,r>0\) such that \[J[\bar y+h]\ge J[\bar y]+c\|h\|_{H^1(a,b)}^2\] for every \(h\in W_0^{1,\infty}(a,b)\) with \(\|h\|_{W^{1,\infty}}<r\). children.title: Convexity-Based Sufficiency
children.top_down_role: Local and global sufficiency families supported by convex variational structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex sufficiency without joint or functional convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T>\pi\), consider fixed-zero-endpoint arcs and \[J[y]=\int_0^T\bigl((y')^2-y^2\bigr)\,dt.\] The integrand is strictly convex in the velocity and \(\bar y\equiv0\) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation. For \(y(t)=c\sin(\pi t/T)\), \[J[y]=\frac{c^2T}{2}\left(\frac{\pi^2}{T^2}-1\right)<0=J[0].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity only in the derivative variable does not make an Euler extremal a minimizer when the state dependence has negative curvature.
assumptions_latex: The admissible class contains the displayed smooth fixed-endpoint arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Convexity of }L\text{ in }v\text{ alone does not imply sufficiency of the Euler equation.}
review_flags: Corrected the builder example: at length \(\pi\) it gives equality rather than failure of minimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Velocity Convexity Alone Is Insufficient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth convex form of first-order sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space, \(\mathcal A\subset X\) be convex, and \(J:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. If \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) and some \(g\in\partial J(\bar u)\) satisfies \[\langle g,u-\bar u\rangle\ge0\quad\forall u\in\mathcal A,\] then \(J(u)\ge J(\bar u)\) for every \(u\in\mathcal A\). With the convex-analytic normal-cone convention, this condition is equivalent to \(0\in\partial J(\bar u)+N_{\mathcal A}(\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex functional on a convex admissible set, the convex first-order condition is sufficient for global minimality.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is proper and convex.
\(\mathcal A\) is convex.
The displayed subgradient and normal-cone objects are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\partial J(\bar u)+N_{\mathcal A}(\bar u)\Longrightarrow\bar u\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u\in\mathcal A}J(u).

notation.meaning: Convex normal cone to the admissible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subgradient Sufficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Convexity Gives Global Quadratic Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative convex sufficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(J\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex on a convex admissible set \(\mathcal A\) and \(\bar u\) satisfies \(0\in\partial J(\bar u)+N_{\mathcal A}(\bar u)\), then \[J(u)\ge J(\bar u)+\frac\mu2\|u-\bar u\|^2\quad\forall u\in\mathcal A.\] Consequently \(\bar u\) is the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong convexity upgrades convex first-order sufficiency to global quadratic growth and uniqueness.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is convex.
\(J\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex for some \(\mu>0\).
\(\bar u\) satisfies the convex first-order condition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global sufficiency for a jointly convex differentiable Lagrangian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J[y]=\int_a^bL(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt\) on a convex fixed-endpoint admissible set \(\mathcal A\). Suppose \((x,v)\mapsto L(t,x,v)\) is differentiable and convex for almost every \(t\), and let \(\bar y\in\mathcal A\) satisfy \[\frac{d}{dt}L_v(t,\bar y,\bar y')=L_x(t,\bar y,\bar y')\] in the weak sense. Then the supporting-hyperplane inequality for \(L\), followed by integration by parts, gives \(J[y]-J[\bar y]\ge0\) for every \(y\in\mathcal A\). Thus \(\bar y\) is a global minimizer; if the integral functional is strictly convex on \(\mathcal A\), this minimizer is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex admissible set and jointly convex Lagrangian, every Euler–Lagrange extremal is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Based Sufficiency

children.title: Fields of Extremals
children.top_down_role: Extremal-field structures supporting comparison arguments.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremal-field variant generated by trajectories through a common point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A central field is a parameterized family of extremals \(y(t,\alpha)\) satisfying \(y(t_0,\alpha)=x_0\) for every \(\alpha\), and forming a regular field on a punctured region where \((t,\alpha)\mapsto(t,y(t,\alpha))\) is locally invertible. The center is not a regular field point because \(D_\alpha y(t_0,\alpha)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A central field consists of extremals through a common point and is regular only away from that center.
assumptions_latex: The parameterized curves solve the Euler–Lagrange equation.
All curves share \((t_0,x_0)\).
Away from the center the parameter dimension equals the state dimension and \(D_\alpha y\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The central family is a regular field precisely on its nonsingular punctured region.}
knowledge_statements.title: Central Field of Extremals

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-coordinate criterion for a differentiable extremal family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(n\)-parameter family of extremals \(y(t,\alpha)\), the columns of \(D_\alpha y(t,\alpha)\) solve the Jacobi system. The family supplies regular local field coordinates exactly where \[\det D_\alpha y(t,\alpha)\ne0.\] At determinant zero the parameter-to-state map is not locally invertible, so locally unique extremal coordinates can fail; conjugate or focal points provide the classical occurrences of this obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter derivatives are Jacobi fields, and their determinant tests local regularity of the extremal field.
assumptions_latex: The Euler–Lagrange system and family are differentiable in \(\alpha\).
The family has as many parameters as the state dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det D_\alpha y\ne0\text{ gives regular local field coordinates; determinant zero is the canonical breakdown boundary.}
review_flags: Determinant zero is stated as failure of the coordinate criterion, not as proof that every conceivable reparameterization fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobi Determinant and Field Breakdown

assumptions_latex: \(L\in C^2\) and is regular in the velocity variable on an open region.
\(y(\cdot,\alpha)\) is a \(C^1\), \(n\)-parameter family of Euler–Lagrange extremals.
\(\det D_\alpha y(t,\alpha)\ne0\) throughout the parameter domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family defines a local field assigning a unique extremal direction and momentum to each covered point \((t,x)\).

notation.meaning: velocity field induced by the family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular local fields generated by an extremal family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A field of extremals on an open set \(U\subset(a,b)\times\mathbb R^n\) is a \(C^1\) family \(y(t,\alpha)\) such that each curve \(t\mapsto y(t,\alpha)\) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equation and the map \((t,\alpha)\mapsto(t,y(t,\alpha))\) is locally invertible onto \(U\). Writing its local inverse parameter as \(\alpha=\alpha(t,x)\), the field induces \[V(t,x):=\partial_ty(t,\alpha(t,x)),\qquad p(t,x):=L_v(t,x,V(t,x)).\] Consequently, each point of \(U\) lies on a locally unique member of the family and inherits its extremal velocity and momentum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular parameterized family of extremals locally assigns a unique extremal velocity and momentum to every point in the covered region.
knowledge_statements.title: Fields of Extremals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the Fields of Extremals leaf, and local invertibility consistently yields the induced velocity and momentum fields. The exact regularity, parameter dimension, and regular-Lagrangian assumptions have no supporting citation or locator.

children.title: Hilbert Invariant-Integral Family
children.top_down_role: Invariant-integral certificates associated with extremal fields.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict form of the invariant-integral comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the Hilbert identity \[J[y]-J[\bar y]=\int_a^bE(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt,\] suppose \(E\ge0\) on the comparison tube and \(E(t,x,v)=0\) only for \(v=q(t,x)\). Equality of actions then forces \(y'=q(t,y)\) almost everywhere. If the field ODE has a unique trajectory from the prescribed initial endpoint, every distinct admissible equal-endpoint competitor satisfies \(J[y]>J[\bar y]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict positivity of excess away from the field slope, plus uniqueness of the field trajectory, yields strict minimality.
assumptions_latex: The Hilbert identity holds for the comparison class.
\(E\ge0\), with equality exactly at \(v=q(t,x)\).
The field ODE has a unique trajectory from the prescribed initial endpoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\ne\bar y\Longrightarrow J[y]>J[\bar y].
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Hilbert-Excess Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness Does Not Ensure Global Path Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological boundary for global Hilbert invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a nonsimply-connected field tube, \(d\omega=0\) gives local exactness but does not force all periods \(\oint_\gamma\omega\) to vanish. Consequently the Hilbert integral can depend on the homotopy class of a path with fixed endpoints. Global endpoint invariance requires exactness, vanishing periods, or restriction to an appropriate simply connected region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed Hilbert form is locally invariant, but global endpoint invariance can fail on a multiply connected tube.
assumptions_latex: \(\omega\) is closed on a possibly nonsimply-connected field tube.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\omega=0\not\Rightarrow\int_\gamma\omega\text{ depends globally only on the endpoints.}
knowledge_statements.title: Closedness Does Not Ensure Global Path Independence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal Fields Generate a Closed Hilbert Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local invariance result underlying the Hilbert integral certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q(t,x)\) be the slope of a sufficiently smooth regular field of Euler–Lagrange extremals and set \(p(t,x)=L_v(t,x,q(t,x))\). Then the Hilbert form \[\omega=\bigl(L(t,x,q)-p\cdot q\bigr)\,dt+p\cdot dx\] is closed. Its integral is invariant under endpoint-fixed homotopies within the field tube; on a simply connected tube, \(\omega=dS\) for a potential \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hilbert one-form of a regular extremal field is closed and is globally exact on a simply connected field tube.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and the regular extremal field are sufficiently differentiable.
\(q\) is induced by Euler–Lagrange extremals.
Simple connectivity is assumed only for global exactness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\omega=0,\qquad \omega=dS\text{ on a simply connected tube.}
knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Fields Generate a Closed Hilbert Form

assumptions_latex: \(L\in C^1(U\times\mathbb R^m)\), where \(U\subset\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^m\) is a simply connected tube.
\(q\in C^1(U;\mathbb R^m)\), and the Hilbert one-form \(\omega\) displayed below is exact on \(U\).
The reference arc satisfies \(\bar y'(t)=q(t,\bar y(t))\), and \(E(t,x,v)\ge 0\) on the comparison domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J[y]-J[\bar y]=\int_a^b E(t,y(t),y'(t))\,dt\ge 0.\]

notation.meaning: Integral functional of an admissible arc.
Hilbert invariant one-form generated by the extremal field.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical first-order Hilbert integral on a simply connected extremal-field tube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^m\) be piecewise \(C^1\), with graph in \(U\), and have the same endpoints as \(\bar y\). Define
\[\omega=\bigl(L(t,x,q)-L_v(t,x,q)\cdot q(t,x)\bigr)\,dt+L_v(t,x,q)\cdot dx.\]
Exactness makes \(\int_y\omega\) depend only on the endpoints. Since \(\bar y'=q(t,\bar y)\), one has \(J[\bar y]=\int_{\bar y}\omega=\int_y\omega\). Consequently,
\[J[y]-J[\bar y]=\int_a^b\!\bigl[L(t,y,y')-L(t,y,q)-L_v(t,y,q)\cdot(y'-q)\bigr]dt=\int_a^b E(t,y,y')\,dt.\]
Thus nonnegativity of \(E\) certifies minimality among these competitors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact Hilbert integral has the same value on equal-endpoint arcs; subtracting it from the action yields the nonnegative Weierstrass excess, certifying minimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Hilbert Invariant-Integral Family

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content and content_kind fit the invariant-integral leaf, and the displayed Hilbert-form identity is mathematically plausible under the stated exactness and excess assumptions. However, the record has no source reference at all, and the supplied inventory contains no source or inspectable locator addressing Hilbert invariant integrals, fields of extremals, or the stated sufficiency certificate. Source support is therefore required before candidate-review acceptance.

children.title: Calibration Methods
children.top_down_role: Comparison-field certificates for global or strong minimality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact uniqueness condition supplementing non-strict calibrated minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \[J[u]-J[\bar u]=\int_\Omega(F-\Phi)(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx,\qquad F-\Phi\ge0.\] If saturation \((F-\Phi)(x,u,
abla u)=0\) almost everywhere forces \(u=\bar u\) almost everywhere within \(\mathcal A\), then \(\bar u\) is the unique global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calibration proves uniqueness when only the calibrated map can have zero calibration gap.
assumptions_latex: The calibration integral is invariant on \(\mathcal A\).
The calibration gap is measurable and nonnegative.
Its almost-everywhere saturation set identifies \(\bar u\) uniquely in \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\ne\bar u\text{ in }\mathcal A\Longrightarrow J[u]>J[\bar u].
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Calibration Gap Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Null-Lagrangian realization of an abstract integral calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\overline\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(C^1\) and define \[\Phi(x,z,P)=\operatorname{div}_xG(x,z)+D_zG(x,z):P.\] Then \(\Phi(x,u,\nabla u)=\operatorname{div}(G(x,u(x)))\), so \[\int_\Omega\Phi(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}G(x,u)\cdot n\,dS.\] This integral is invariant on a class with common trace. If \(\Phi\le F\) on the admissible jets and equality holds along \(\bar u\), then \(\bar u\) is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A total-divergence minorant is a calibration because its integral is fixed by the boundary trace.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\) is a bounded Lipschitz domain.
The competitors have a common trace and the chain rule and divergence theorem apply.
\(\Phi\le F\) on admissible jets, with equality almost everywhere along \(\bar u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J[u]\ge J[\bar u]\quad\forall u\in\mathcal A.
knowledge_statements.title: Divergence Calibration Representation

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a class of admissible maps with fixed boundary data, and \(J[u]=\int_\Omega F(x,u(x),\nabla u(x))\,dx\).
A measurable integrand \(\Phi\) satisfies \(\int_\Omega\Phi(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx=C\) for every \(u\in\mathcal A\).
\(\Phi(x,z,\xi)\le F(x,z,\xi)\) on the admissible state-gradient set, with equality almost everywhere along \((\bar u,\nabla\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J[u]\ge C=J[\bar u]\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathcal A.\]

notation.meaning: Admissible comparison class with prescribed boundary data.
Calibration integrand whose integral is invariant on the comparison class.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract integral calibration covering comparison fields and null-Lagrangian certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A calibration for \(\bar u\in\mathcal A\) is an integrand \(\Phi\) whose integral is invariant on \(\mathcal A\), lies pointwise below the energy density, and saturates that bound on \(\bar u\). For every \(u\in\mathcal A\),
\[J[u]=\int_\Omega F(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx\ge\int_\Omega\Phi(x,u,\nabla u)\,dx=C.\]
Saturation gives
\[J[\bar u]=\int_\Omega F(x,\bar u,\nabla\bar u)\,dx=\int_\Omega\Phi(x,\bar u,\nabla\bar u)\,dx=C.\]
Hence \(J[u]\ge J[\bar u]\) throughout \(\mathcal A\); strict domination away from the calibrated state yields the corresponding strict-minimality conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calibration is an invariant comparison integral lying below the energy and touching it on the reference map; integration then certifies global minimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Calibration Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A calibration certificate is the correct content_kind for this leaf, and the non-strict global-minimality implication follows formally from invariant integral, domination, and saturation. Nevertheless, no relevant source or inspectable locator is supplied. In addition, the domains of \(\Omega\), \(z\), and \(\xi\), the measure and regularity setting, and the admissible state-gradient set are not defined; the final strict-minimality claim also lacks a precise quantified strictness condition ensuring a strict integral gap for every distinct competitor. An authoritative calibration or null-Lagrangian source and a fully specified formulation are required.
